ELA.overview: English 12 moves chronologically from Beowulf to Modernism, with college essays in the fall and a six-week Senior Research Paper in the spring. Read each text (or the assigned portion) before teaching it, read key passages aloud together, and insist on textual evidence for every claim. Keep a steady rhythm: read, annotate, discuss, then write — and grade writing with the 4-level rubrics in each week's key. Preview mature content flagged in the prep notes.

weeks.prep: Find Brian Doyle's 'Joyas Voladoras' (widely anthologized; originally in The American Scholar) and read it first. Print the UC Personal Insight Question list (admission.universityofcalifornia.edu). Set up a writing notebook.
misconceptions: Students think a college essay must describe a dramatic achievement. Ordinary moments told with specific detail and honest reflection are usually stronger.
Telling instead of showing ('I am hardworking'). Ask: 'What would a camera have seen?' and have them write that scene.
All story, no reflection (or the reverse). Aim for roughly half narrative, half insight.

days.guide: Read 'Joyas Voladoras' aloud together. Model one annotation (e.g., the hummingbird heart detail) and say how the concrete fact carries feeling; the student finds three more and writes a tone paragraph. Check that each annotation names both the detail and the emotion it creates.

questions.q: How does Doyle move through the essay, and where does it end up?
questions.a: From the tiny, fast-beating hearts of hummingbirds to the enormous heart of the blue whale, and finally to the human heart — the essay turns scientific facts into a meditation on how fragile and vulnerable our emotional hearts are.

questions.q: Describe the essay's tone in two words with evidence.
questions.a: Wondering and tender — the precise, awed facts about animal hearts build to a gentle, aching close about human love and pain.

days.guide: Explain that the best essay stories come from specific memories. The student completes all four lists of 10, then stars the three with the most sensory detail. Check: can they tell each starred story with a specific time and place?

questions.q: What makes a memory a strong candidate for an essay?
questions.a: It is specific (a particular moment, place, people), shows the student acting or changing, and leads to genuine reflection.

days.guide: With two highlighters, mark story sentences and insight sentences in a model essay and discuss the ratio. The student freewrites 300 words on one starred story ending with what it taught them.

questions.q: What is the difference between a narrative sentence and a reflective sentence?
questions.a: A narrative sentence reports what happened ('I dropped the tray'); a reflective sentence explains meaning ('I learned that asking for help is a skill, not a weakness').

days.guide: Model three openings: participial phrase ('Gripping the rail, I…'), subordinate clause ('When the power failed, …'), prepositional phrase ('Behind the barn, …'). The student revises the freewrite so no two consecutive sentences start the same way; check by listing first words.

questions.q: Rewrite 'I walked into the kitchen. I saw my grandmother.' with varied openings.
questions.a: Sample: 'Walking into the kitchen, I saw my grandmother at the stove.' or 'When I walked into the kitchen, my grandmother was already at the stove.'

questions.q: Identify the opening type: 'After the game ended, we sat in silence.'
questions.a: Subordinate (adverb) clause.

days.guide: The student reads aloud; you ask two 'I want to know more about…' questions. They submit the freewrite with a 3-sentence voice reflection.

questions.q: What is 'voice' in a personal essay?
questions.a: The writer's distinct personality on the page — word choice, rhythm, humor, and perspective that sound like that specific person.

weeks.assessment_key: Inventory: complete if all 40 items listed and 3 starred. Freewrite rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Detail — 4 = concrete sensory details place the reader in a specific moment; 2 = mostly general statements. Reflection — 4 = ending offers a genuine, specific insight, not a cliché; 2 = moral tacked on ('it made me stronger'). Proficient: 3 in both.

weeks.prep: Read the UC PIQ page and tips with the student. Set up a word processor with word count visible. Note: each PIQ response is limited to 350 words and students choose 4 of 8.
misconceptions: Writing about the prompt topic instead of about themselves. Every paragraph should reveal the student's actions, thinking, or growth.
Two PIQs that show the same trait. Plan four responses that together show different sides.
Treating cutting as losing content. Cutting filler usually makes the voice stronger.

days.guide: Read all 8 prompts aloud and chart which starred stories fit which prompts. The student chooses four and explains why each shows something different.

questions.q: How many UC PIQs must a student answer and what is the word limit?
questions.a: Four of the eight, each up to 350 words.

days.guide: Model the moment → action → result → meaning structure by outlining one story together. The student drafts PIQ #1. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: In 'moment → action → result → meaning,' what goes in 'meaning'?
questions.a: What the experience shows about the student — what they learned, value, or will bring to college.

days.guide: The student drafts PIQ #2 on a different prompt. Check: does it show a different quality than #1? Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: If PIQ #1 shows leadership, what might PIQ #2 show?
questions.a: A different side, e.g., intellectual curiosity, creativity, or overcoming a challenge.

days.guide: Model cutting 15%: delete 'very,' 'really,' 'in order to,' change passive to active, remove repeated ideas. The student records word counts before and after.

questions.q: Tighten: 'In order to really improve, the project was redone by me.'
questions.a: 'To improve, I redid the project.'

days.guide: Review drafts with the checklist (specific? answers the prompt? shows impact?). The student writes a revision plan for each.

questions.q: What makes a revision plan useful?
questions.a: It names specific changes (e.g., 'replace paragraph 2 summary with the moment in the lab').

weeks.assessment_key: Two PIQ drafts under 350 words plus revision plan. Rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = each draft answers its prompt directly, uses a specific moment, shows the student's action and impact, ends with insight; revision plan lists concrete changes. 3 = clear and specific with minor generalities. 2 = summary-heavy or off-prompt. 1 = incomplete or over the limit.

weeks.prep: Have all PIQ drafts printed. Prepare a mechanics checklist (comma splices, run-ons, its/it's, possessives). Optional: Common App prompts for students applying beyond UC.
misconceptions: Replacing clichés with fancier clichés. Replace abstractions with concrete actions or images.
Comma splices (two independent clauses joined by only a comma). Fix with a period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction.
Rehearsed, memorized interview answers. Aim for natural conversation with specific examples.

days.guide: The student drafts PIQs #3–4, including one on academic interest or community. Check they total four distinct responses.

questions.q: Which PIQ prompts address academics or community?
questions.a: Prompt 6 (an academic subject that inspires you) and Prompt 7 (making your school or community a better place).

days.guide: Model replacing 'I am passionate about science' with an action ('I spent three Saturdays recalibrating our pH sensors'). The student hunts clichés in all four drafts.

questions.q: Revise the cliché 'This experience made me who I am today.'
questions.a: Replace with a specific change, e.g., 'Now I'm the one who volunteers to stay late and fix the inventory spreadsheet.'

days.guide: Teach the checklist, then model reading backwards sentence by sentence. The student edits all four. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Fix: 'I love chemistry, it explains everything.'
questions.a: 'I love chemistry; it explains everything.' or 'I love chemistry because it explains everything.'

questions.q: Its or it's: 'The team lost ___ best player.'
questions.a: its

days.guide: Conduct a 10-minute mock interview: 'Tell me about yourself' plus one question per PIQ. Give feedback on specificity and eye contact.

questions.q: What makes a strong answer to 'Tell me about yourself'?
questions.a: A brief, specific story connecting interests, an example, and future goals — not a résumé list.

days.guide: The student submits four final PIQs (≤350 words each) and a reflection paragraph on their biggest revision. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should the reflection name?
questions.a: One concrete change (e.g., cutting a summary paragraph and adding a scene) and why it improved the essay.

weeks.assessment_key: College-essay rubric, each criterion 1–4 (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Specificity — concrete moments, names, details. Insight — reflection shows self-awareness and growth. Voice — sounds like the student. Conventions — no comma splices, run-ons, or apostrophe errors; each ≤350 words. Proficient: 12/16 with no criterion below 3 for conventions.

weeks.prep: Obtain Beowulf (Gummere on Project Gutenberg or Heaney). Read the first half yourself. Find a short article on the Sutton Hoo ship burial (British Museum site). Parental note: battle violence is frequent but not graphic by modern standards. Line numbers differ by translation — use your edition's.
misconceptions: Reading Beowulf as a fantasy adventure only. Point out the poem's mix of pagan heroic values (fame, gold, revenge) and Christian commentary (God, Cain).
Kennings misread as metaphors in general. A kenning is a compressed two-word metaphorical name: 'whale-road' for the sea.
Assuming the boast is arrogance. In the heroic code a boast is a public promise the hero must fulfill.

days.guide: Read a Sutton Hoo overview and list warrior values (loyalty, courage, generosity, fame, revenge). Then read 'The Seafarer' and mark where Christian ideas take over.

questions.q: Where do pagan and Christian ideas meet in 'The Seafarer'?
questions.a: The speaker describes the hardships and loneliness of sea life and fleeting earthly glory (an older heroic/elegiac view), then turns to praising God and seeking a lasting home in heaven.

questions.q: Name three values of the Anglo-Saxon warrior culture.
questions.a: Loyalty to one's lord, courage in battle, and a lord's generosity (ring-giving); also fame and revenge.

days.guide: Read the opening through Beowulf's arrival at Heorot. The student collects 8 kennings and translates them. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Translate: whale-road, ring-giver, bone-house.
questions.a: The sea; a king or lord; the body.

questions.q: Why does Grendel attack Heorot?
questions.a: He is enraged by the joyful sounds of feasting and songs of creation in the hall; the poem says he descends from Cain.

days.guide: Read the Unferth exchange and the fight. Model one paragraph structure: claim, quotation, explanation. The student writes the paragraph citing two quotations.

questions.q: What does Unferth accuse Beowulf of, and how does Beowulf respond?
questions.a: Of losing a swimming contest with Breca. Beowulf says he won, killed sea-monsters, and taunts Unferth for killing his own brothers.

questions.q: How does Beowulf defeat Grendel?
questions.a: Bare-handed — he tears off Grendel's arm, and Grendel flees to die.

days.guide: Read Grendel's mother. The student charts the two battles side by side and discusses revenge. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does Grendel's mother attack and whom does she kill?
questions.a: To avenge her son; she kills Aeschere, Hrothgar's trusted counselor.

questions.q: What happens to Hrunting?
questions.a: Unferth's sword fails against her; Beowulf kills her with a giant's sword he finds in her lair.

days.guide: Give a 20-question quiz, then a timed 20-minute response on glory vs. duty. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who is king of the Danes, and what is his hall?
questions.a: Hrothgar; Heorot.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz sample answers: Hrothgar, Danes; Heorot; Grendel descended from Cain; Beowulf is a Geat, Hygelac's nephew; Unferth and the Breca contest; arm torn off; Aeschere killed; Hrunting fails; giant's sword. Timed paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear claim (glory, duty, or both), two well-chosen pieces of evidence, explanation linking evidence to the heroic code; 3 = clear claim with one well-explained piece; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Finish reading Beowulf. Borrow John Gardner's Grendel (read chapter 1 yourself first; it contains crude language and violence — preview). Prepare the essay prompt.
misconceptions: Thinking Beowulf's last fight was simply heroic. Discuss whether he acts wisely as an aging king, leaving his people vulnerable.
Commas around appositives: essential appositives take no commas; nonessential ones do.
Organizing an essay by plot. Organize by idea (each paragraph proves a part of the thesis).

days.guide: Read the dragon episode and death. The student annotates shifts from triumph to elegy. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What wakes the dragon?
questions.a: A thief steals a jeweled cup from its treasure hoard.

questions.q: How does the tone change at the end?
questions.a: It becomes elegiac: mourning Beowulf, the funeral pyre and barrow, and forebodings that the Geats will be attacked now that their king is gone.

days.guide: Read Wiglaf's speech. The student writes a paragraph on loyalty and the failed comitatus. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Wiglaf tell the thanes who fled?
questions.a: He shames them: they took their lord's gifts but deserted him; their families will lose their rights and the Geats will be dishonored and endangered.

days.guide: Read Gardner's chapter 1; the student fills a two-column chart comparing Grendel's portrayal. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Gardner's Grendel differ from the poem's?
questions.a: Gardner's Grendel narrates in first person — lonely, sardonic, intelligent — whereas the poem presents him from outside as a monstrous descendant of Cain.

days.guide: Teach appositives using Beowulf's epithets. The student writes five punctuated sentences. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Punctuate: Beowulf the son of Ecgtheow sailed to Denmark.
questions.a: Beowulf, the son of Ecgtheow, sailed to Denmark.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word explanatory essay on good leadership and the limits of heroism. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the ending suggest about heroism's limits?
questions.a: Even the greatest hero ages and dies; his death leaves his people vulnerable, suggesting individual heroism cannot secure a society forever.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanatory essay rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Thesis — 4 = defines good leadership (courage, generosity, protecting one's people) and states a clear claim about heroism's limits. Evidence — 4 = at least 3 well-chosen quotations (e.g., Hrothgar's generosity, the dragon fight, Wiglaf's speech). Organization — 4 = idea-based paragraphs with transitions. Proficient: 3 in each.

weeks.prep: Get a modern verse translation of The Canterbury Tales. Find an audio recording of the first 18 lines in Middle English. Prepare a vocabulary list (estate, pilgrimage, satire, irony, etc.).
misconceptions: Taking the narrator's praise at face value. Chaucer's narrator often praises flaws naively — verbal irony.
Assuming medieval satire attacks the Church as a whole. Chaucer satirizes corrupt individuals while presenting ideal figures like the Parson.
Thinking Middle English is Old English. Old English (Beowulf) needs full translation; Middle English is readable with a glossary.

days.guide: Explain the three estates and the Black Death. Listen to the Middle English opening and compare to translation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where are the pilgrims going and why?
questions.a: To Canterbury to the shrine of St. Thomas Becket.

questions.q: What contest does the Host propose?
questions.a: Each pilgrim tells tales on the journey; the best storyteller wins a free supper at the Tabard Inn.

days.guide: Read the Knight, Prioress, Monk, Friar. The student charts ideal role vs. behavior. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does the Monk fall short of his ideal role?
questions.a: He loves hunting, fine horses, and fur-trimmed clothes, ignoring the rules of monastic life.

questions.q: How is the Knight presented?
questions.a: As an ideal: brave, humble, courteous, coming straight from campaigns in his stained tunic.

days.guide: Read the Wife of Bath, Parson, Miller, Summoner, Pardoner. The student marks verbal irony. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Pardoner selling?
questions.a: Fake relics (e.g., pig's bones) and pardons.

questions.q: How is the Parson different?
questions.a: Poor and genuinely good; he practices what he preaches.

days.guide: Teach Old→Middle→Modern English changes. The student translates four lines. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Translate 'Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote.'
questions.a: When April with its sweet showers.

days.guide: The student writes a modern satirical portrait; give vocabulary quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is verbal irony in Chaucer's portraits?
questions.a: The narrator praises a character for traits that actually reveal a flaw.

weeks.assessment_key: Satirical portrait rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = 20 lines, contemporary type, narrator's ironic praise exposes gap between ideal and reality, specific details. Vocabulary quiz answers: estate = social class; satire = ridicule to expose faults; irony = contrast between expectation and reality.

weeks.prep: Read the Pardoner's Tale, the Wife of Bath's Tale, and the Gawain beheading-game and girdle sections first. Parental preview: the Wife of Bath's Tale begins with a knight raping a maiden; plan to discuss it directly and seriously. Prepare the unit test.
misconceptions: Missing the Pardoner's double irony: he preaches against greed while openly admitting he preaches for profit — then tries to sell to the pilgrims anyway.
Reading the Wife of Bath's Tale as simply feminist or simply anti-woman. It both challenges (women's desire for sovereignty) and reinforces (the hag's ideal wife ending) medieval views.
Vague pronouns ('this shows'). Always follow 'this' with a noun: 'this irony shows…'

days.guide: Read the Pardoner's Prologue and Tale aloud. Ask the student to state the moral and then explain why the teller makes it ironic; check that they mention both the tale and the teller.

questions.q: Summarize the plot of the Pardoner's Tale.
questions.a: Three rioters set out to kill Death; an old man directs them to a tree where they find gold. The youngest goes to town and buys poison; the other two plot to kill him. They stab him on his return, then drink the poisoned wine and all die.

questions.q: What is the double irony?
questions.a: The Pardoner's theme is 'greed is the root of evil' (Radix malorum est cupiditas), yet he admits he preaches it only to make money — and then tries to sell relics to the pilgrims.

days.guide: Read the Wife of Bath's Tale; address the opening crime plainly. The student answers both parts of the question with evidence.

questions.q: What does the knight learn women most desire?
questions.a: Sovereignty — mastery over their husbands.

questions.q: How does the tale end, and how does it both challenge and reinforce medieval views?
questions.a: Given the choice between an old, faithful wife or a young, possibly unfaithful one, the knight lets her choose; she becomes beautiful and faithful. It challenges male authority by valuing women's sovereignty, but reinforces ideals by ending with an obedient, pleasing wife.

days.guide: Read the beheading game and girdle episode. The student lists how chivalric ideals (courage, honesty, courtesy, chastity) are tested.

questions.q: What is Gawain's one failing?
questions.a: He keeps the green girdle from the lady instead of giving it to his host under their exchange-of-winnings agreement, because he believes it will save his life.

questions.q: How is he punished?
questions.a: At the Green Chapel the Green Knight feints twice and then gives him only a small nick on the neck for hiding the girdle; Gawain wears the girdle afterward as a sign of his fault.

days.guide: Model fixing vague pronouns in a sample paragraph. The student revises a paragraph so every 'it/this/they' has a clear antecedent.

questions.q: Revise: 'The Pardoner and the Host argue, and he gets angry.'
questions.a: 'The Pardoner and the Host argue, and the Host gets angry.'

days.guide: Give the unit test (identification, short answer, 40-minute comparative essay). Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Which two texts pair well for 'testing society's ideals'?
questions.a: E.g., Gawain (chivalry tested by temptation) and Beowulf (heroic code tested by age and failed loyalty).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test: identification (Hrothgar, Grendel's mother, Wiglaf, the Pardoner, the Wife of Bath, the Green Knight, Bertilak) and short answers per the questions above. Comparative essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = thesis naming two texts and the ideals tested, balanced evidence from both, analysis of how each text judges its society, organized by idea; 3 = solid comparison with uneven evidence; 2 = summary of two texts with little comparison; 1 = one text only.

weeks.prep: Download Macbeth from the Folger Shakespeare Library (free). Read Act I. Find a short source on James I, witchcraft, and the Gunpowder Plot. Parental note: the play contains murder and violence.
misconceptions: Reading line by line as prose and getting lost. Read to punctuation, not to line endings.
Thinking the witches control Macbeth. They prophesy; Macbeth and Lady Macbeth choose to act.
Iambic pentameter = 10 syllables, 5 unstressed–stressed feet; students may count syllables but ignore stress.

days.guide: Present background on the Globe and James I. Model marking stresses in 'So foul and fair a day I have not seen.' The student scans three lines.

questions.q: Scan 'So foul and fair a day I have not seen.'
questions.a: so FOUL / and FAIR / a DAY / i HAVE / not SEEN — five iambs.

days.guide: Read I.1–I.3 aloud with parts. Discuss 'Fair is foul' as equivocation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What do the witches prophesy to Macbeth and Banquo?
questions.a: Macbeth will be Thane of Cawdor and king; Banquo will father kings though not be one.

questions.q: What does 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' suggest?
questions.a: Appearances deceive; good and evil are confused — the play's theme of equivocation.

days.guide: Read I.4–I.5. Paraphrase Lady Macbeth's soliloquy line by line. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Lady Macbeth fear about her husband?
questions.a: He is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness' to take the quickest way to the crown.

questions.q: What does she ask the spirits?
questions.a: To 'unsex' her and fill her with cruelty so no remorse stops her.

days.guide: Read I.6–I.7. The student charts the arguments in 'If it were done.' Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are Macbeth's reasons not to kill Duncan?
questions.a: He is Duncan's kinsman, subject, and host; Duncan is a virtuous king; and only 'vaulting ambition' drives him.

questions.q: How does Lady Macbeth change his mind?
questions.a: She questions his manhood and courage and gives him a plan to drug the guards and blame them.

days.guide: The student recites 10 lines; give the Act I quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who is named Prince of Cumberland?
questions.a: Malcolm.

weeks.assessment_key: Act I quiz: witches' prophecies; Macbeth made Thane of Cawdor; Malcolm named heir; Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me' soliloquy; 'vaulting ambition'; manhood argument. Recitation rubric: 4 = 10 lines word-perfect with meaningful pauses and emphasis; 3 = 1–2 slips; 2 = several prompts needed; 1 = not memorized.

weeks.prep: Read Acts II–III. Select a filmed production (e.g., the 2010 Patrick Stewart PBS version or the 1979 Ian McKellen/Judi Dench version) and preview the banquet scene. Make a motif tracker chart (blood, sleep, darkness).
misconceptions: Treating the Porter scene as irrelevant comedy. It is comic relief that also echoes damnation and equivocation.
Quotations dropped without commentary. Every quotation needs explanation.
Assuming Macbeth always hesitates. After Duncan, he plans Banquo's murder alone.

days.guide: Read II.1–II.2. The student starts the motif tracker. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the dagger represent?
questions.a: A 'dagger of the mind' — his guilty, overheated imagination drawing him toward murder.

questions.q: What does Macbeth hear after the murder?
questions.a: A voice crying 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep.'

days.guide: Read II.3–II.4. Explain comic relief and unnatural events. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What unnatural events follow Duncan's murder?
questions.a: Darkness by day, an owl killing a falcon, Duncan's horses eating each other.

days.guide: Read III.1–III.2. The student writes a paragraph comparing Macbeth's reasoning. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does Macbeth want Banquo dead?
questions.a: Banquo suspects him, and the witches said Banquo's descendants would be kings — Macbeth's crown is 'fruitless' and his sceptre 'barren.'

days.guide: Read III.3–III.6; watch the banquet scene. Discuss staging the ghost. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who escapes the murderers?
questions.a: Fleance, Banquo's son.

days.guide: The student writes a 400-word motif paragraph with four quotations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a blood quotation from Act II.
questions.a: 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?' (II.2)

weeks.assessment_key: Motif paragraph rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = topic sentence claims how the motif develops (e.g., blood shifts from honor to guilt), 4+ quotations with act/scene/line, commentary after each, progression across acts. Proficient: 3+ quotations, clear commentary.

weeks.prep: Read Acts IV–V. Choose two filmed productions and identify the same scene (e.g., V.1 or V.5) in each.
misconceptions: Taking the apparitions literally like Macbeth. Each prophecy is technically true but misleading.
Thinking Lady Macbeth was always strong. Track her collapse in V.1.
Comparing films only on 'which is better.' Compare specific choices.

days.guide: Read IV.1. The student explains each apparition. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What do the three apparitions say?
questions.a: An armed head: beware Macduff. A bloody child: none of woman born shall harm Macbeth. A crowned child with a tree: Macbeth is safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane.

questions.q: How do two of these come true?
questions.a: Malcolm's soldiers carry Birnam Wood branches as camouflage; Macduff was 'untimely ripped' from his mother's womb (born by Caesarean).

days.guide: Read IV.2–IV.3. Compare responses to loss. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Macduff say when told to 'dispute it like a man'?
questions.a: 'I shall do so; / But I must also feel it as a man.'

days.guide: Read V.1. Analyze prose and reversal of 'a little water clears us.' Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Lady Macbeth say about her hand?
questions.a: 'Out, damned spot!' and 'All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.'

days.guide: Read V.2–V.8. The student performs and analyzes 'Tomorrow.' Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What view of life does Macbeth express?
questions.a: Life is meaningless — 'a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.'

days.guide: Watch the same scene in two versions and fill in the chart. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name one dimension for comparing productions.
questions.a: Setting, casting, cuts, or tone.

weeks.assessment_key: Production chart rubric (4 levels): 4 = chart compares setting, casting, cuts, and tone with specific details from both versions, and a claim about faithfulness supported by the text; 3 = all categories with general notes; 2 = only one production detailed; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print Sonnets 18, 29, 73, 116, 130. Gather Macbeth notes and motif tracker. Prepare an argument-essay rubric.
misconceptions: A counterclaim that is a straw man. Present the strongest opposing view fairly before rebutting.
Switching to past tense when discussing literature. Use the literary present: 'Macbeth kills Duncan.'
Assuming the volta in a Shakespearean sonnet always comes at line 9. It often comes at the couplet (line 13).

days.guide: Model a thesis and counterclaim for 'Who is more responsible for Duncan's murder?' The student drafts a thesis, counterclaim, and evidence outline.

questions.q: Give a sample thesis and counterclaim.
questions.a: Thesis: Macbeth bears more responsibility because he imagines the murder before Lady Macbeth speaks and commits further murders on his own. Counterclaim: Lady Macbeth manipulates him by attacking his manhood in I.7.

days.guide: The student drafts the 900–1,200-word essay with (Act.Scene.Line) citations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How should a Macbeth quotation be cited in MLA?
questions.a: By act, scene, and line: (1.7.25–28).

days.guide: Read Sonnets 18, 73, 130; label quatrains, volta, couplet. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Sonnet 130 parody the Petrarchan blazon?
questions.a: It denies each conventional comparison ('My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun') and then insists in the couplet that his love is as rare as any woman 'belied with false compare.'

questions.q: What three images of aging does Sonnet 73 use?
questions.a: Autumn (yellow leaves), twilight, and a dying fire.

days.guide: The student revises for transitions and literary present. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Correct: 'Macbeth was haunted by Banquo's ghost.'
questions.a: 'Macbeth is haunted by Banquo's ghost.'

days.guide: The student submits the essay and an original sonnet. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of a Shakespearean sonnet?
questions.a: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay (W.11-12.1) rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Claim — precise, arguable. Evidence — 5+ cited quotations. Counterclaim — strongest opposing view fairly stated and rebutted. Organization/style — transitions, literary present, MLA citations. Sonnet: 14 lines, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, mostly iambic pentameter, a turn at line 9 or 13.

weeks.prep: Read 'A Modest Proposal' (Project Gutenberg) and Canto 1 of 'The Rape of the Lock.' Pick an appropriate modern satire (e.g., a news-satire article) and preview it. Parental note: Swift's subject (eating babies) is deliberately shocking.
misconceptions: Thinking Swift really proposed eating children. The persona's proposal is ironic; Swift's targets are English landlords and Irish indifference.
Confusing Horatian (gentle) and Juvenalian (bitter) satire. Pope is Horatian; Swift is Juvenalian.
Writing satire without a target. Every satire needs a real problem and implied solution.

days.guide: Explain the Irish famine context. Read paragraphs 1–10; mark the calm, logical tone. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the proposer suggest?
questions.a: That poor Irish families sell their one-year-old children to be eaten by the wealthy.

days.guide: Finish the essay. The student charts techniques and identifies Swift's real proposals. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are Swift's real proposals?
questions.a: In the paragraph beginning 'Therefore let no man talk to me of other expedients,' he lists them: taxing absentee landlords, using only Irish goods, rejecting foreign luxuries, and landlords showing mercy to tenants.

questions.q: Why does the proposer claim no personal profit?
questions.a: His youngest child is nine and his wife is past childbearing.

days.guide: Read Pope excerpt. Explain mock epic. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What trivial event does Pope treat as epic?
questions.a: A baron cutting a lock of Belinda's hair.

questions.q: Explain 'Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux.'
questions.a: The list puts Bibles alongside cosmetics and love letters, satirizing a society that treats religion as just another vanity.

days.guide: Analyze a modern satire: target, technique, real argument; compare to Swift. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What three things should be identified in any satire?
questions.a: The target, the technique (irony, exaggeration, understatement), and the real argument.

days.guide: The student writes a 500-word modest proposal with a deadpan persona. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does 'deadpan' mean?
questions.a: Delivering absurd ideas with a completely serious tone.

weeks.assessment_key: Satire rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Persona — consistent deadpan voice. Technique — 3+ satirical devices. Target — clear real issue and hidden real solution. Conventions. Proficient: 3 in each.

weeks.prep: Print the Romantic poems. Read Wordsworth's 'The World Is Too Much With Us' for the timed explication. Prepare an AP-style 6-point rubric.
misconceptions: Treating explication as summary. Explication analyzes how figurative language, sound, and structure create meaning.
Reading 'The Tyger' and 'The Lamb' as children's poems. They are paired poems of innocence and experience.
Misreading Keats's urn as a living scene. The urn freezes moments permanently.

days.guide: Read the three Blake poems aloud. The student compares innocence and experience and annotates 'London.' Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who made the Lamb, according to the speaker?
questions.a: God, who 'calls himself a Lamb' — Christ.

questions.q: What are 'mind-forg'd manacles' in 'London'?
questions.a: Mental chains — limits on thought imposed by society, institutions, and people's own minds.

days.guide: Read Wordsworth's definition and 'Tintern Abbey' lines. The student writes about a changed place. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Complete Wordsworth's definition: 'spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings…'
questions.a: '…it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.'

questions.q: How long has the speaker been away in 'Tintern Abbey'?
questions.a: Five years.

days.guide: Read 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn.' Discuss permanence. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the irony in 'Ozymandias'?
questions.a: The king commands 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' but nothing remains except a broken statue and empty sand.

questions.q: What does the urn say?
questions.a: 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.'

days.guide: Teach explication (literal, figurative, sound, structure, theme). Explicate 'Ozymandias' together. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What sonnet form does 'Ozymandias' use?
questions.a: A sonnet with an unusual rhyme scheme blending Petrarchan and Shakespearean patterns.

days.guide: Give the 40-minute timed explication of 'The World Is Too Much With Us.' Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the speaker criticize?
questions.a: Materialism — 'Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers'; we are out of tune with nature.

weeks.assessment_key: AP-style 6-point rubric: Thesis (0–1): defensible interpretation of how the poem's devices create meaning (e.g., Wordsworth contrasts commercial life with nature). Evidence and commentary (0–4): specific references — 'Getting and spending,' the Petrarchan octave/sestet turn at 'Great God! I'd rather be / A Pagan,' allusions to Proteus and Triton. Sophistication (0–1). Proficient: 4/6.

weeks.prep: Obtain Frankenstein (1818 text, Project Gutenberg). Read the 1831 introduction and Letters 1–4 and chapters 1–5. Make a vocabulary log template.
misconceptions: Calling the creature 'Frankenstein.' Victor Frankenstein is the creator; the creature is unnamed.
Skipping the frame. Walton's letters mirror Victor's ambition.
Assuming the novel is a horror story only. It explores responsibility and ambition.

days.guide: Read the 1831 introduction and Walton's letters. The student notes parallels. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What prompted Mary Shelley's novel?
questions.a: A ghost-story contest with Byron, Percy Shelley, and Polidori at Lake Geneva in 1816.

questions.q: How does Walton mirror Victor?
questions.a: Both pursue glory through discovery, ignoring danger and isolation.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–3. Track influences. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Which professor inspires Victor at Ingolstadt?
questions.a: M. Waldman.

days.guide: Read chapters 4–5. Annotate Gothic diction. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Victor react when the creature opens its eyes?
questions.a: Horror and disgust — he flees and abandons the creature.

days.guide: Use context and roots to define 15 words. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define 'lassitude.'
questions.a: Weariness; lack of energy.

days.guide: Give the reading quiz and Prometheus paragraph. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why 'The Modern Prometheus'?
questions.a: Prometheus stole fire for humanity and was punished; Victor seizes the power of creating life and suffers.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: Walton writes to sister Margaret; Victor from Geneva; mother dies of scarlet fever; Ingolstadt; Waldman; creation in November. Paragraph rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = explains the myth and connects to Victor with quotations.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 6–17. Prepare seminar questions and norms (cite the text, build on others). Seminar can be parent + student or a co-op group.
misconceptions: Concluding the creature is purely a victim or purely a villain. Push for both: he is shaped by rejection, yet he still chooses to murder William and frame Justine.
Treating the seminar as a debate to 'win.' Remind the student the goal is shared understanding — they should ask questions and build on others' points.
Forgetting the creature's own crimes when sympathizing with him. Have the student list his choices (William, Justine) next to the injustices done to him.

days.guide: Read chapters 6–8. Discuss Victor's silence at the trial; ask the student whether his reasons justify it and to cite one line.

questions.q: Why is Justine accused?
questions.a: The picture (miniature) William wore is found in her pocket — the creature planted it.

questions.q: Why doesn't Victor speak up?
questions.a: He believes no one would believe his story and would think him mad, so he protects himself while Justine is executed.

days.guide: Read chapters 9–10. Connect the Alps to Romantic sublime. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where does Victor meet the creature?
questions.a: On the glacier near Montanvert/Mont Blanc (the Mer de Glace).

days.guide: Read chapters 11–13. The student lists what the creature learns. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Which books shape the creature?
questions.a: Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and The Sorrows of Werther.

questions.q: Who are the De Laceys?
questions.a: An exiled family — blind old father, Felix, Agatha — joined by Safie; the creature learns language by watching them.

days.guide: Read chapters 14–17 and hold the seminar. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens when the creature reveals himself to the De Laceys?
questions.a: The blind father is kind, but Felix attacks him; the family flees and the creature burns the cottage.

questions.q: What does the creature demand?
questions.a: A female companion.

days.guide: The student writes a 300-word reflection. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong seminar reflection?
questions.a: It cites a specific idea from someone else and explains how it changed or confirmed the student's view.

weeks.assessment_key: Seminar participation rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = cites text 3+ times, asks questions, builds on others. Reflection: 4 = cites a specific idea, explains its effect on thinking, references text.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 18–24 and Walton's final letters before the week. Prepare a theme-map template and a 10-question final reading quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking the creature kills Victor. Victor dies of illness and exhaustion aboard Walton's ship; have the student find the passage.
Confusing semicolons and colons. A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences; a colon introduces a list, explanation, or quotation after a complete sentence.
Listing themes without showing how they interact. Ask: 'How does theme A cause or intensify theme B?'

days.guide: Read chapters 18–20 together, pausing at the destruction of the female creature. The student writes Victor's reasons in his own words and analyzes how Victor misreads the 'wedding-night' threat as aimed at himself.

questions.q: Why does Victor destroy the female creature?
questions.a: He fears she might be even more malignant, might refuse the creature's promise to leave humanity, and that the pair could produce a 'race of devils.'

questions.q: What does the creature threaten, and how does Victor misunderstand it?
questions.a: 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night.' Victor assumes the creature means to kill him, not Elizabeth.

days.guide: Read chapters 21–23. The student builds a chart of every death, its cause, and whom Victor blames; discuss where Victor accepts responsibility and where he deflects it.

questions.q: List the deaths and causes.
questions.a: William (strangled by the creature), Justine (executed after being framed), Clerval (strangled by the creature), Elizabeth (strangled on the wedding night), Alphonse (dies of grief), and later Victor (illness/exhaustion). Earlier, Caroline died of scarlet fever.

days.guide: Read chapter 24 and Walton's final letters. Discuss why Walton turns back and how the creature's last speech reframes the story.

questions.q: Why does Walton turn back?
questions.a: His crew threatens mutiny and demands to return home if the ice frees them; he reluctantly agrees, unlike Victor choosing others' lives over ambition.

questions.q: What does the creature plan at the end?
questions.a: To go to the northernmost extremity, build a funeral pyre, and destroy himself; he disappears 'borne away by the waves.'

days.guide: Show three long Shelley sentences and label the semicolon, colon, and dash in each. The student writes six original sentences about the novel (two each) and reads them aloud.

questions.q: Punctuate: Victor had one goal to create life
questions.a: Victor had one goal: to create life.

questions.q: Join correctly: The creature asked for a companion Victor refused in the end
questions.a: The creature asked for a companion; Victor refused in the end.

days.guide: The student builds the theme map with six quotations and arrows showing interaction, then takes the final reading quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give two interacting themes with an example.
questions.a: Responsibility and isolation: Victor's refusal to care for the creature isolates it, and its isolation drives the murders that isolate Victor.

weeks.assessment_key: Final reading quiz: 1) Female creature destroyed in the Orkneys. 2) Threat: 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night.' 3) Clerval murdered; Victor jailed in Ireland. 4) Elizabeth killed on wedding night. 5) Alphonse dies of grief. 6) Victor pursues creature to the Arctic. 7) Walton's crew demands return. 8) Victor dies aboard ship. 9) Creature mourns over Victor. 10) Creature plans his own funeral pyre. Theme map rubric (4 levels): 4 = two themes, six accurate quotations from across the novel, clear explanation of how they interact; 3 = accurate but interaction thin; 2 = quotations without analysis; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find a contemporary article on AI or gene editing (CommonLit, a library database, or a reputable newspaper) and read it first. Print the argument rubric and the Purdue OWL MLA page.
misconceptions: A thesis that just names a 'monster.' A nuanced thesis explains why and under what conditions — e.g., what Victor does or fails to do.
Forcing the modern connection. The paragraph must name specific parallels (a creator's responsibility, consent, unintended consequences).
MLA errors: citing the novel without page or chapter, or listing the article without its container. Check each citation against OWL.

days.guide: Read the article together. The student lists three specific ways it echoes Victor's choices; check that each names a behavior, not just a topic.

questions.q: Give one way current technology debates echo Victor.
questions.a: Developers creating powerful systems before thinking through responsibility for how they affect people — as Victor creates life and then abandons it.

days.guide: Model turning a simple claim into a nuanced thesis. The student writes one and outlines three body paragraphs with evidence assigned.

questions.q: Give a nuanced thesis on 'Who is the real monster?'
questions.a: Victor becomes the true monster not by creating life but by abandoning it; his refusal of responsibility turns a benevolent being toward violence.

days.guide: The student drafts the 1,200-word essay, including one paragraph that connects the novel to the article. Check that quotations are introduced and explained.

questions.q: Where should the modern connection go?
questions.a: In a later body paragraph, after the literary argument is established, so the novel stays the focus.

days.guide: Read the draft and give two strengths and two priorities. The student revises and checks every in-text citation and the Works Cited.

questions.q: Write an MLA Works Cited entry for a Project Gutenberg Frankenstein.
questions.a: Shelley, Mary. Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. 1818. Project Gutenberg, www.gutenberg.org.

days.guide: The student submits the final essay and scores it against the rubric with a sentence of evidence per criterion. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a self-assessment useful?
questions.a: Specific evidence for each score and one goal for the next essay.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary argument rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Thesis — nuanced and arguable. Evidence — 6+ well-chosen quotations from across the novel. Analysis — explains how evidence proves the claim. Modern connection — specific and integrated. MLA — correct in-text citations and Works Cited. Proficient: 3 in each.

weeks.prep: Gather notes, vocabulary logs, and the writing portfolio. Write the semester final: 3 short passages (Beowulf, Macbeth, Frankenstein) with multiple-choice and short-answer items, plus a synthesis essay prompt.
misconceptions: Mixing up literary periods. Anchor each text to a date and one trait (e.g., Beowulf — Anglo-Saxon, oral heroic code).
Defining 'overreacher' too broadly. An overreacher pursues power or knowledge beyond human limits and is destroyed by it.
Writing a portfolio reflection as a list. Compare a specific early sentence or paragraph with a later one.

days.guide: The student builds a timeline placing each text with one defining trait of its period. Check order and traits orally. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Put in order with periods: Frankenstein, Beowulf, Macbeth, The Canterbury Tales, A Modest Proposal.
questions.a: Beowulf (Anglo-Saxon), Canterbury Tales (Middle English/Medieval), Macbeth (Renaissance/Elizabethan–Jacobean), A Modest Proposal (Enlightenment/Neoclassical, 1729), Frankenstein (Romantic, 1818).

days.guide: Discuss the overreacher archetype across Beowulf, Macbeth, and Victor. The student takes notes with one quotation per character.

questions.q: How is Macbeth an overreacher?
questions.a: He seizes the crown beyond his rightful place, and his ambition destroys him.

questions.q: Is Beowulf an overreacher?
questions.a: Arguably in his final fight: as an old king he insists on fighting the dragon largely alone, dies, and leaves his people exposed.

days.guide: The student takes a practice test on appositives, pronoun reference, and semicolons/colons; review errors immediately. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Punctuate: Victor a scientist from Geneva abandons his creation
questions.a: Victor, a scientist from Geneva, abandons his creation.

days.guide: Administer the final (about 2 hours). Grade using the key. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name two traits of Romanticism.
questions.a: Emphasis on emotion and imagination, and on nature and the sublime (also the individual).

days.guide: The student selects two best pieces and writes a 400-word reflection comparing early and later writing. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong portfolio reflection?
questions.a: Specific before/after examples and an explanation of what skill improved.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key: passages identified (Beowulf, Macbeth, Frankenstein) with period traits; short answers drawn from weekly quizzes (e.g., Hrothgar/Heorot; 'vaulting ambition'; Walton's frame). Synthesis essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = thesis comparing two works, balanced evidence, analysis of period/archetype; 3 = clear comparison; 2 = summary; 1 = one work. Portfolio reflection rubric: 4 = specific examples of growth; 2 = general statements.

weeks.prep: Print 'Dover Beach,' 'My Last Duchess,' 'Ulysses,' and a 'Goblin Market' excerpt. Choose an unseen dramatic monologue for the quiz (e.g., Browning's 'Porphyria's Lover' — preview: it depicts a murder — or Tennyson's 'Tithonus').
misconceptions: Confusing the poet with the speaker. In a dramatic monologue the speaker is a character, often unreliable.
Missing the silent listener (auditor). Ask: who is being spoken to, and why?
Reading 'Dover Beach' as only about the sea. The sea is an image of retreating religious faith.

days.guide: Give a short overview of industrialization, empire, and Darwin. Read 'Dover Beach' aloud; the student annotates images of retreating faith and the final plea.

questions.q: What is the 'Sea of Faith' and what is happening to it?
questions.a: Religious faith, once full; now the speaker hears only its 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar.'

questions.q: What does the speaker ask at the end?
questions.a: 'Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!' — personal fidelity in a world with no certainty, where 'ignorant armies clash by night.'

days.guide: Read 'My Last Duchess' aloud twice. Ask the student to infer what happened and cite lines; check that they notice what the Duke reveals.

questions.q: What happened to the Duchess?
questions.a: The Duke implies he had her killed: 'I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together.'

questions.q: Who is the listener and why is it ironic?
questions.a: An envoy arranging the Duke's next marriage — the Duke reveals his jealous, controlling nature to the person negotiating his new bride.

days.guide: Read 'Ulysses.' Compare its striving ideal with Beowulf's heroism in a two-column chart. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the poem's final resolution?
questions.a: 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.'

questions.q: How is Ulysses like and unlike Beowulf?
questions.a: Both are aging heroes who seek one last challenge; Ulysses seeks experience and knowledge, while Beowulf fights to protect his people.

days.guide: Review features: speaker, auditor, occasion, revealing more than intended. The student drafts a 30-line monologue; check that the listener is implied, not addressed by stage directions.

questions.q: What makes a dramatic monologue 'dramatic'?
questions.a: A single speaker addresses a silent listener in a specific situation, revealing character, often unintentionally.

days.guide: Give the quiz on an unseen monologue; the student shares their monologue aloud. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: In 'My Last Duchess,' what does the Duke's comment about his 'nine-hundred-years-old name' reveal?
questions.a: His pride; he resented that the Duchess valued simple pleasures as much as his ancient family name.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (for the chosen poem): identify the speaker, the silent auditor, the situation, and at least one example of irony where the speaker reveals more than intended. Monologue rubric (4 levels): 4 = 30 lines, distinct speaker voice, implied listener and occasion, the speaker unintentionally reveals a flaw, vivid diction; 3 = clear monologue, revelation less subtle; 2 = speech without listener; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Download A Doll's House (Project Gutenberg). Read the play. Prepare seminar norms and the question.
misconceptions: Seeing Torvald's pet names as simple affection. List them and ask what kind of creature each names — a pet or a child — to show how he diminishes Nora.
Calling Nora's forgery selfish. Point out she borrowed secretly to pay for the trip that saved Torvald's life, and has been repaying it herself.
Judging the ending from personal feelings alone. Require a line from each act to support any claim in seminar.

days.guide: Read Act I. The student lists every pet name Torvald uses and what each suggests. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name pet names Torvald uses.
questions.a: 'Little lark,' 'squirrel,' 'little spendthrift,' 'little featherhead' — diminishing names for a pet or child.

questions.q: What is Nora's secret?
questions.a: She borrowed money from Krogstad to fund a trip to Italy that saved Torvald's health, forging her father's signature.

days.guide: Read Act II. Analyze the tarantella. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does Nora dance the tarantella so wildly?
questions.a: To distract Torvald from the letterbox where Krogstad's letter waits; it expresses her desperation.

days.guide: Read Act III. Annotate shifts in power. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Torvald react to the letter, then to the returned bond?
questions.a: He calls her a liar and criminal; when the bond is returned he forgives her — showing his love was about his reputation.

questions.q: What does Nora realize?
questions.a: She has been a 'doll-wife,' as she was her father's 'doll-child,' and must leave to understand herself.

days.guide: Hold the seminar: heroic, selfish, or both? Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a line supporting Nora's choice.
questions.a: She says she has duties to herself that are as sacred as those to her husband and children.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word essay on Nora's transformation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Trace Nora's transformation in one sentence.
questions.a: Nora moves from a playful doll-wife to a woman who recognizes she must stand alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric (4 levels): 4 = cites all three acts, builds on others, poses questions. Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = traces change across all three acts with quotations, explains causes (Krogstad's threat, Torvald's reaction), analyzes the door slam.

weeks.prep: Download The Importance of Being Earnest (Project Gutenberg) and choose a filmed production (e.g., 2002 film or 1952 film). Prepare the timed essay prompt.
misconceptions: Dismissing the comedy as frivolous. Show how each joke exposes Victorian hypocrisy about marriage, class, and respectability.
Explaining epigrams literally. Have the student name the expected saying or value and show how Wilde inverts it.
Comparing Ibsen and Wilde only by plot. Ask how each mode — realism vs. comedy — makes the critique land differently.

days.guide: Read Act I. The student collects five epigrams and explains each paradox. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Explain 'The truth is rarely pure and never simple.'
questions.a: It reverses the cliché 'the plain and simple truth' and hints at the lies both men tell.

questions.q: Explain Lady Bracknell's line about losing parents.
questions.a: 'To lose one parent… may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness' — absurdly treating tragedy as social failing.

days.guide: Read Act II. Analyze Bunburying. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is Bunburying?
questions.a: Algernon's invented invalid friend, Bunbury, used as an excuse to escape social obligations — a satire of double lives.

days.guide: Read Act III. Discuss the absurd ending. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How is Jack's identity resolved?
questions.a: Miss Prism had left baby Jack in a handbag at Victoria Station; he is Algernon's older brother and was christened Ernest.

days.guide: Watch a scene and evaluate performance choices. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How can performance heighten Wilde's comedy?
questions.a: Deadpan delivery and exaggerated reactions emphasize absurdity.

days.guide: Give the 45-minute comparison essay. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What modes do Ibsen and Wilde use?
questions.a: Ibsen uses realism; Wilde uses comedy and satire.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = thesis on how realism and comedy each critique marriage and respectability; evidence from both plays; analysis of how mode affects the critique. 3 = clear comparison; 2 = summary; 1 = one play only.

weeks.prep: Borrow Things Fall Apart. Read Part One. Print Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden.' Parental preview: the novel includes violence, wife-beating, and the killing of a child.
misconceptions: Taking Kipling's poem as neutral information. Treat it as a primary source of imperialist ideology and analyze its assumptions and audience.
Seeing Okonkwo as representative of all Igbo values. Point to characters such as Obierika and Nwoye and to community judgments that question him.
Treating proverbs as decoration. Ask what each proverb accomplishes in its conversation (persuading, softening criticism, showing respect).

days.guide: Read Kipling as a primary source. The student analyzes its assumptions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Kipling describe colonized peoples?
questions.a: 'Half-devil and half-child' — a racist assumption that they need Western rule.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–5. Build Okonkwo's profile. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Okonkwo fear?
questions.a: Being like his father, Unoka — lazy, in debt, and considered weak.

days.guide: Read chapters 6–9. Analyze Ikemefuna's death. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does Okonkwo strike Ikemefuna?
questions.a: He is afraid of being thought weak.

questions.q: How does it affect Nwoye?
questions.a: Something 'gave way inside him'; it alienates him from his father.

days.guide: Collect 8 proverbs and explain their function. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Explain 'Proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten.'
questions.a: Proverbs make speech persuasive and graceful.

days.guide: Give reading quiz and paired-text paragraph. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does Achebe's Umuofia answer Kipling?
questions.a: By showing a complex society with law, religion, and art — refuting the idea that Africans were uncivilized.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Unoka; Amalinze the Cat; Ikemefuna from Mbaino; Ezinma; Week of Peace violation. Paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim with evidence from both texts.

weeks.prep: Read Parts Two and Three. Print 'The Second Coming.' Prepare debate format. Parental note: Okonkwo's suicide occurs at the end.
misconceptions: Blaming only colonialism or only Okonkwo. Require evidence for both forces before the student takes a side in the debate.
Missing the irony of the Commissioner's book title. Ask what 'pacification' and 'primitive' mean after reading a whole novel about Umuofia's complex society.
Debating without rebuttal. Each speaker must answer the other side's strongest evidence, not just repeat their own.

days.guide: Read chapters 14–19. Discuss exile. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why is Okonkwo exiled?
questions.a: His gun accidentally explodes at Ezeudu's funeral and kills Ezeudu's son; he must leave for seven years to his mother's village, Mbanta.

days.guide: Analyze Nwoye's conversion. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What draws Nwoye to Christianity?
questions.a: The hymn and the questions about twins thrown away and Ikemefuna's death.

days.guide: Read chapters 20–25. Annotate the ending. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens to Okonkwo?
questions.a: He kills a court messenger; the others let the remaining messengers escape; he hangs himself.

questions.q: What is the Commissioner's planned title?
questions.a: The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

days.guide: Read 'The Second Coming.' Discuss Achebe's title. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Quote the source line.
questions.a: 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.'

days.guide: Hold the debate. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give evidence for 'his own rigidity.'
questions.a: He refuses to adapt, uses violence, and alienates his son.

weeks.assessment_key: Debate rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear position, 3+ textual citations, effective rebuttal.

weeks.prep: Obtain Achebe's 'An Image of Africa' (anthology/library) and the opening river-journey section of Heart of Darkness (Project Gutenberg). Parental preview: Conrad uses racist language and imagery, which is the subject of Achebe's critique — discuss it directly.
misconceptions: Dismissing Achebe as merely offended, or dismissing Conrad as simply racist without engaging the argument. Evaluate premises and evidence.
Confusing Marlow's views with Conrad's. Achebe argues Conrad provides no alternative frame; others argue the narrative frame creates distance — weigh both.
Vague lens statements. Name the lens (postcolonial) and what it asks.

days.guide: Read the river-journey passage aloud. The student notes how Africans are described (and not allowed to speak); check that they quote specific words.

questions.q: How are Africans portrayed in the passage?
questions.a: Largely as a mass of bodies and noise — e.g., 'a whirl of black limbs' — rather than as individuals with speech and thought.

days.guide: Read 'An Image of Africa.' The student outlines premises, evidence, and conclusion. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is Achebe's central claim?
questions.a: That Heart of Darkness dehumanizes Africans, using Africa as a backdrop for a European's mind, and that Conrad was a racist (a 'thoroughgoing racist'); thus the novel shouldn't be celebrated uncritically.

days.guide: Model evaluating an argument: strongest premise, weakest premise, counterargument. The student writes a one-page evaluation.

questions.q: Give a counterargument to Achebe.
questions.a: The novel critiques imperial brutality and greed, and Marlow's framed narration may distance Conrad from his narrator's views.

days.guide: The student drafts 800 words on Things Fall Apart as an answer to colonial literature; check for specific contrasts. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give one way Things Fall Apart answers Heart of Darkness.
questions.a: It shows Africans speaking, reasoning, and governing from the inside, and ends by exposing the Commissioner's reductive view.

days.guide: The student revises for precise claims and integrated quotations and submits with a lens statement. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Write a one-sentence lens statement.
questions.a: 'I read Things Fall Apart through a postcolonial lens, asking how it restores voice and complexity to a culture colonial writing reduced.'

weeks.assessment_key: Postcolonial essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise thesis, evidence from Achebe's novel and at least one colonial text (Kipling or Conrad), fair treatment of the critical debate, integrated quotations, MLA. 3 = clear argument with thinner evidence; 2 = summary; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Get a public library card and learn the database login (Gale, EBSCO). Set up a research notebook. Print a CRAAP test checklist.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic instead of a question ('climate change'). Narrow to an open, arguable question with a place, group, or policy.
Trusting sources that look professional. Apply the CRAAP test to every source and record the reasons.
Collecting many sources and reading none deeply. Keep the four strongest and read them closely.

days.guide: Brainstorm five topics; model narrowing one into a question. The student writes an arguable question; check it can't be answered with a simple fact.

questions.q: Narrow 'social media' into a research question.
questions.a: 'Should California high schools restrict student phone use during the school day to improve learning?'

days.guide: Model a database search with keywords and Boolean operators. The student finds six sources and records citations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does AND do in a database search?
questions.a: Narrows results to sources containing both terms.

days.guide: Explain CRAAP. The student evaluates each source and keeps four. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does CRAAP stand for?
questions.a: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

days.guide: The student writes the one-page proposal. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a working hypothesis?
questions.a: A tentative answer to the research question that the research may revise.

days.guide: Hold a 10-minute conference; the student revises the question. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should feedback focus on?
questions.a: Whether the question is focused, arguable, and researchable.

weeks.assessment_key: Proposal rubric (4 levels): 4 = focused arguable question, significance, hypothesis, plan with 4+ credible sources. Source chart: CRAAP scores with reasons.

weeks.prep: Bookmark Purdue OWL MLA (9th ed.). Gather sources. Prepare note-card or digital-note templates.
misconceptions: Patchwriting — swapping synonyms while keeping the source's structure. Read, cover the source, write from memory, then compare.
Notes without page numbers. Require source tag and page on every note so citations are easy later.
Annotations that only summarize. Each annotation must also evaluate credibility and state how the source will be used.

days.guide: Model paraphrasing a passage by reading, covering, writing, and comparing. The student paraphrases three passages and fixes borrowed phrasing.

questions.q: What is patchwriting?
questions.a: Copying a source's sentence structure and changing a few words — a form of plagiarism.

days.guide: Model tagging notes (Q/P/S) with source and page. The student reads two sources and makes 15 notes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: When should you quote rather than paraphrase?
questions.a: When the exact wording is memorable, authoritative, or the subject of analysis.

days.guide: The student reads two more sources and adds 15 notes, flagging agreement and disagreement. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why flag disagreements?
questions.a: They reveal the debate the paper can enter.

days.guide: Teach MLA 9 containers. The student writes four entries. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Order of MLA core elements?
questions.a: Author. Title. Container, Other contributors, Version, Number, Publisher, Date, Location.

days.guide: The student submits the annotated bibliography. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What goes in a 100-word annotation?
questions.a: Summary, evaluation of credibility, and how it will be used.

weeks.assessment_key: Annotated bibliography rubric (4 levels): 4 = 6–8 correctly formatted MLA entries, alphabetized with hanging indents, each annotation summarizes, evaluates, and states use. 3 = minor format errors; 2 = summary only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Create a synthesis-matrix template (subtopics × sources). Prepare a consent script for interviews or surveys.
misconceptions: Outlining source by source. Organize by subtopic so each section synthesizes several sources.
A thesis that is too broad or merely factual. Test it: could a reasonable person disagree? Is it specific about who, what, and why?
Leading survey questions. Rewrite each question neutrally and pilot it with one person first.
