days.guide: Model a synthesis matrix. The student fills it in and identifies a gap. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does a synthesis matrix reveal?
questions.a: Where sources agree, disagree, or are silent.

days.guide: Draft three thesis versions and choose the most specific. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Which is stronger: 'Phones affect learning' or 'California high schools should restrict phones during class because research links them to lower attention'?
questions.a: The second — it is specific and arguable.

days.guide: The student conducts an interview or survey (5+ responses). Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why is primary research valuable?
questions.a: It adds original evidence and local perspective.

days.guide: The student writes a full-sentence outline including counterargument. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What goes in a counterargument section?
questions.a: The strongest opposing view and a rebuttal.

days.guide: Meet to confirm each section has at least two sources. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why two sources per section?
questions.a: It shows synthesis rather than relying on one voice.

weeks.assessment_key: Checkpoint rubric (4 levels): 4 = specific arguable thesis; full-sentence outline; each section with 2+ sources; counterargument; primary research recorded.

weeks.prep: Have the outline, notes, and synthesis matrix at hand. Block 60–90 minutes daily for drafting. Print a list of signal phrases.
misconceptions: 'Quote-dumping' — quotations with no commentary. Require at least two sentences of commentary per quotation.
Conclusions that only repeat the introduction. Ask 'So what?' — implications, recommendations, or open questions.
A straw-man counterargument. Represent the strongest opposing source accurately before rebutting.

days.guide: Model an introduction: hook, context, and thesis as the last sentence. The student drafts their introduction using at least two signal phrases; check that the thesis matches the approved outline.

questions.q: Give three signal phrases.
questions.a: 'According to…,' 'X argues that…,' 'As Y points out,…'

days.guide: The student drafts the first major section (2–3 pages) following the outline. Check a page: each quotation should be introduced, cited, and followed by two sentences of commentary.

questions.q: What is commentary?
questions.a: The writer's explanation of how the evidence supports the claim — not a restatement of the quotation.

days.guide: The student drafts the second section, integrating primary research. Show how to report survey or interview results with numbers and context.

questions.q: How should survey results be reported?
questions.a: With counts or percentages and the sample: 'Seven of ten parents surveyed (70%) said…' plus a note on limits.

days.guide: The student drafts the counterargument section. Ask them to read the opposing source's strongest point aloud first. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a fair counterargument?
questions.a: It states the opposing view accurately and at its strongest, with a source, before rebutting with evidence.

days.guide: The student drafts the conclusion and submits the complete rough draft. Skim for missing sections or citations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should a conclusion do?
questions.a: Explain the implications of the findings and why they matter, without simply repeating the introduction.

weeks.assessment_key: Rough-draft checkpoint (4 levels): 4 = complete draft with introduction and thesis, two body sections with commentary, primary research, fair counterargument, conclusion with implications, in-text citations throughout; 3 = complete with thin commentary in places; 2 = one section missing or uncited; 1 = substantially incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print a research-paper rubric for the reader. Arrange a reader (parent, mentor, tutor) for Day 2. Have the source notes available for the plagiarism self-check.
misconceptions: Treating revision as proofreading. Revise argument and organization first; edit sentences last.
Faulty parallelism in lists. Make every list item the same grammatical form.
Unintentional plagiarism from notes. Compare every paraphrase with the original source.

days.guide: Model a reverse outline on one page. The student writes one sentence per paragraph and cuts or moves paragraphs that don't advance the thesis.

questions.q: What is a reverse outline used for?
questions.a: To see the draft's actual structure and find paragraphs that repeat, drift, or are out of order.

days.guide: The reader scores the draft with the rubric and writes comments. The student picks the three highest-impact revisions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How should feedback be prioritized?
questions.a: Argument and structure first, then evidence and commentary, then style and mechanics.

days.guide: The student makes the three revisions and adds transitions between major sections. Read the transitions aloud together. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Write a transition between sections.
questions.a: 'While these studies show phones reduce attention, they leave open whether restrictions actually improve grades.'

days.guide: The student edits sentence by sentence for parallelism, hyphenation, and commas, then checks every paraphrase against notes.

questions.q: Fix: 'Students like reading, to write, and math.'
questions.a: 'Students like reading, writing, and doing math.'

questions.q: Hyphenate correctly: 'a well known study' vs. 'the study is well known.'
questions.a: 'a well-known study' (before the noun); 'the study is well known' (after).

days.guide: The student formats in MLA and submits the revised draft with tracked changes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What goes in the MLA heading?
questions.a: Student name, instructor, course, and date, flush left and double-spaced; last name and page number top right.

weeks.assessment_key: Revised draft rubric (4 levels): 4 = tracked changes show substantive revision (structure, evidence, counterargument), improved transitions, clean mechanics, correct MLA format; 3 = real revision plus editing; 2 = mostly surface edits; 1 = little change.

weeks.prep: Have the final draft ready. Install slide software. Find a model abstract (e.g., from a student research journal) to show.
misconceptions: Writing the abstract as an introduction. An abstract summarizes the whole paper, including findings.
Charts without sources or labels. Every visual needs a title, labeled axes, and a source caption.
Planning to read the paper aloud as a presentation. Storyboard key ideas, not paragraphs.

days.guide: Show a model abstract and label its four parts. The student writes a 150-word abstract. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What four elements does an abstract include?
questions.a: Question, method, findings, and significance.

days.guide: The student reads the paper aloud to proofread, fixes errors, and submits the final 8–10 page paper. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why proofread aloud?
questions.a: Hearing the text catches missing words, awkward sentences, and errors the eye skips.

days.guide: The student turns one key finding into a chart or infographic. Check the title, labels, and source caption. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What must a chart caption include?
questions.a: What the chart shows and its source.

days.guide: The student storyboards the 10-minute presentation section by section, with a time estimate for each. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: List the storyboard sections.
questions.a: Hook, question, findings, counterargument, conclusion, Q&A.

days.guide: The student writes a research reflection. Discuss it briefly. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should the reflection address?
questions.a: What surprised them, what they'd do differently, and what question remains.

weeks.assessment_key: Senior Research Paper rubric (each 1–4): Thesis (specific, arguable); Research (credible, varied sources including primary research); Synthesis and commentary; Counterargument and rebuttal; Organization and transitions; MLA citations and Works Cited; Conventions. Proficient: 21/28 with no score below 2.

weeks.prep: Print Brooke 'The Soldier,' Owen 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth,' Sassoon 'Suicide in the Trenches,' and Eliot 'Prufrock.' Parental preview: Owen depicts a gas death graphically; Sassoon's poem depicts a soldier's suicide — check in with the student emotionally.
misconceptions: Reading all WWI poems as anti-war. Brooke's 'The Soldier' (1914) is idealistic and patriotic; Owen and Sassoon write from later trench experience.
Assuming Prufrock is literally going to a party and proposing. The 'overwhelming question' is never asked; the poem dramatizes paralysis and self-consciousness.
Missing form as meaning: 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' is a sonnet — a love-poem form — used for mass death.

days.guide: Read 'The Soldier' and 'Dulce et Decorum Est' aloud. The student charts imagery and attitude; check that they quote both poems.

questions.q: How does Brooke imagine a soldier's death?
questions.a: As a noble gift: 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England.'

questions.q: What is 'the old Lie' in Owen's poem?
questions.a: 'Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori' — it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country (from Horace).

days.guide: Read 'Suicide in the Trenches' and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth.' Explain how Owen subverts the sonnet; ask what Sassoon blames.

questions.q: How does 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' subvert the sonnet?
questions.a: It uses the sonnet's lyrical form for a funeral without rites: 'What passing-bells for these who die as cattle? / Only the monstrous anger of the guns.'

questions.q: Whom does Sassoon's final stanza attack?
questions.a: The 'smug-faced crowds' at home who cheer soldiers marching off but never face 'the hell where youth and laughter go.'

days.guide: Read 'Prufrock' aloud. The student annotates fragmented images and signs of paralysis. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What simile opens the poem and what does it suggest?
questions.a: The evening 'spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherised upon a table' — numbness and passivity.

questions.q: Quote a line showing Prufrock's paralysis.
questions.a: 'Do I dare / Disturb the universe?' or 'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons.'

days.guide: Discuss allusions; compare with Browning's monologue. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Prufrock say about Hamlet?
questions.a: 'No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be; / Am an attendant lord' — he sees himself as a minor character.

questions.q: How is Prufrock unlike the Duke?
questions.a: The Duke is confident and controlling; Prufrock is anxious and indecisive, and his monologue is internal and fragmented.

days.guide: Give the 40-minute timed comparison of Owen and Brooke. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: State a comparative thesis.
questions.a: Brooke presents death as a noble gift to England, while Owen's graphic gas attack exposes that idea as 'the old Lie.'

weeks.assessment_key: Timed essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = thesis contrasting attitudes toward war and sacrifice, close analysis of imagery and form in both poems (Brooke's sonnet of idealized England; Owen's gas imagery 'As under a green sea' and the Horace allusion), context; 3 = clear comparison; 2 = summary; 1 = one poem only.

weeks.prep: Download The Metamorphosis (Project Gutenberg). Read it. Find two short critical interpretations (e.g., in a library database or SparkNotes-style critical overviews). Parental note: the story is bleak and ends in Gregor's death.
misconceptions: Asking 'What insect is he really?' Redirect to how realistically everyone responds to the absurd premise.
Reading the ending as purely happy. Point out that the family's relief comes immediately after Gregor's lonely death.
Picking an interpretation by preference. Require at least three pieces of evidence from different parts of the story.

days.guide: Read Part I. Ask why Gregor worries about his job; the student marks deadpan narration. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Gregor worry about first?
questions.a: Missing his train and losing his job as a traveling salesman — he supports his family and their debts.

days.guide: Read Part II. The student tracks each family member's treatment of Gregor. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens with the apple?
questions.a: His father pelts him with apples; one lodges in his back and rots, a lasting wound.

questions.q: How does Grete's role change?
questions.a: She first feeds him with care, then becomes impatient and dominant over his care.

days.guide: Read Part III. Analyze the ending's tone. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Grete say about Gregor?
questions.a: That they must get rid of 'it' — she no longer considers it her brother.

questions.q: What happens after Gregor dies?
questions.a: The family takes a tram to the countryside, feeling hopeful; the parents notice Grete has become a young woman and think of finding her a husband.

days.guide: Read two interpretations; the student chooses the more convincing one with evidence. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give an economic reading in one sentence.
questions.a: Gregor is valued only as a breadwinner; when he can't work, his family sees him as a burden.

days.guide: The student writes a 700-word essay. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a sample thesis.
questions.a: Kafka's absurd transformation exposes a realistic truth: Gregor's family loves him only as long as he is useful.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = thesis connecting absurd premise to realistic theme (alienation, economic worth, family duty), evidence from all three parts, analysis of narration and ending. 3 = clear with thinner evidence; 2 = summary; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Obtain 'Shooting an Elephant,' 'Politics and the English Language,' and the 1984 Appendix ('The Principles of Newspeak'). Collect two current euphemism examples from news or ads. Prepare the Modernism unit test.
misconceptions: Reading 'Shooting an Elephant' as a hunting story. It is about imperialism's effect on the oppressor.
Treating Orwell's rules as absolute. Rule 6 says to break them rather than write something barbarous.
Thinking euphemism is always dishonest. It becomes political when it hides wrongdoing.

days.guide: Read 'Shooting an Elephant.' Ask why Orwell shoots the elephant; the student explains the indictment of imperialism. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does Orwell shoot the elephant?
questions.a: Because a crowd of Burmese expects it; he admits he did it 'solely to avoid looking a fool.'

questions.q: What realization does he state?
questions.a: 'When the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys.'

days.guide: Read 'Politics and the English Language'; the student outlines structure and evaluates. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: List Orwell's six rules.
questions.a: 1) No stale figures of speech; 2) short word over long; 3) cut words when possible; 4) active over passive; 5) no foreign/jargon word if an everyday one exists; 6) break any rule sooner than say anything barbarous.

questions.q: Give an example of political euphemism from the essay.
questions.a: 'Pacification' for bombing villages and driving out inhabitants.

days.guide: Read the Newspeak Appendix; connect to modern euphemisms. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is Newspeak's purpose?
questions.a: To narrow the range of thought so that dissent becomes literally unthinkable.

days.guide: The student revises a research-paper paragraph using Orwell's rules. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Revise: 'It is believed by many that utilization of phones is impactful.'
questions.a: 'Many people believe phones affect learning.'

days.guide: Give the Modernism unit test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name two Modernist techniques.
questions.a: Fragmentation and stream of consciousness/interior monologue.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key: Owen's 'old Lie'; Brooke's 'foreign field'; Prufrock's paralysis; Metamorphosis family response; Orwell's reason for shooting; six rules; Newspeak's purpose. Short essays rubric (4 levels): thesis, evidence, analysis.

weeks.prep: Slides, a timer, and a phone to record video. Have the research paper and storyboard ready.
misconceptions: Text-heavy slides. One idea per slide, with images or charts and minimal text.
Rehearsing silently in one's head. Rehearse out loud, standing, with a timer.
Avoiding the hardest questions. List them deliberately and prepare evidence.

days.guide: Show one text-heavy slide and redesign it together. The student builds 10–12 one-idea slides. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the one-idea-per-slide rule?
questions.a: Each slide makes one point supported by an image or chart and very little text.

days.guide: The student writes speaker notes and rehearses transitions, timing the talk at 10–12 minutes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should speaker notes contain?
questions.a: Key points and transitions in brief phrases, not a full script.

days.guide: Record a full rehearsal and watch it together. The student counts filler words and notes pacing and eye contact. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How can filler words be reduced?
questions.a: Pause silently instead of saying 'um' or 'like'; practice transitions.

days.guide: The student lists the 8 hardest questions and drafts evidence-based answers. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give one likely hard question.
questions.a: 'What evidence contradicts your thesis, and why aren't you persuaded?'

days.guide: Hold a dress rehearsal for a family member; the student revises from feedback. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What feedback is most useful?
questions.a: Specific moments where clarity, pacing, or visuals broke down.

weeks.assessment_key: Rehearsal self-critique rubric (4 levels): 4 = specific notes on timing, filler counts, eye contact, and slide clarity with a concrete revision plan; 3 = accurate but general; 2 = superficial; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Invite at least two adults for the panel and print scoring sheets (content, delivery, visuals, Q&A). Choose a TED talk to evaluate. Find a local paper's op-ed guidelines.
misconceptions: Defending rather than engaging during Q&A. Acknowledge good points and explain with evidence.
Evaluating a speaker only on style. Assess reasoning and evidence too.
Writing the op-ed like an academic paper. Use a hook, short paragraphs, plain language, and one clear argument.

days.guide: The student presents to the panel and answers 5 minutes of questions. Panelists score with the rubric. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How should the student answer a question they can't fully answer?
questions.a: Acknowledge the limit and explain how they would investigate it.

days.guide: Watch the talk. The student evaluates reasoning, evidence, and rhetoric in a page. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What three features should the evaluation address?
questions.a: Reasoning (logic), evidence (quality and sources), and rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos).

days.guide: Review the panel sheets together. The student writes a full response to the toughest question. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why write a response after the defense?
questions.a: To give a fuller, evidence-based answer and show reflection.

days.guide: The student writes a 650-word op-ed for a general audience and submits it. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does an op-ed differ from a research paper?
questions.a: It is short, opens with a hook, uses plain language, and makes one clear argument with a call to action.

days.guide: The student writes a reflection on the research process from question to defense. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should the reflection include?
questions.a: Key decisions, challenges, growth, and what they'd do differently.

weeks.assessment_key: Defense panel rubric (each 1–4): Content (clear thesis, evidence); Delivery (pacing, eye contact); Visuals (clear, sourced); Q&A (thoughtful, evidence-based). Op-ed rubric (4 levels): 4 = about 650 words, hook, clear claim, 2+ pieces of evidence, plain style, call to action.

weeks.prep: Gather all writing from the year. Choose Google Sites or a binder. Schedule the final conference.
misconceptions: Treating the portfolio as a collection only. Each piece needs a short note on why it was chosen.
Cosmetic revision. Revise argument, structure, or evidence — not just word choice.
Vague goals ('read more'). Make goals specific and measurable.

days.guide: The student selects five pieces and writes a sentence for each explaining the choice. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What five pieces go in the portfolio?
questions.a: A PIQ, a literary analysis, a timed write, the research paper, and a creative piece.

days.guide: The student revises one earlier piece and lists the changes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a revision meaningful?
questions.a: Changes to thesis, structure, or evidence that improve the argument.

days.guide: The student writes a 'letter to my future self' using a quotation from a text that mattered. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How should the quotation be integrated?
questions.a: Introduce it, quote it accurately with citation, and explain why it matters to them.

days.guide: The student publishes the portfolio with a reflective introduction. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What belongs in the reflective introduction?
questions.a: An overview of growth with specific examples from the pieces.

days.guide: Hold the final conference; the student sets three goals. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a specific reading goal.
questions.a: 'Read one classic novel per month this summer and keep a one-page response for each.'

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric (each 1–4): Selection (five required pieces with rationales); Revision (substantive, documented); Reflection (specific evidence of growth); Presentation (organized, polished). Proficient: 12/16.

HSS.overview: Semester 1 is American Government and Civics; Semester 2 is Economics. Ground each lesson in a primary source or real data (the Constitution, Supreme Court opinions, the California Voter Guide, FRED, BLS), have the student explain ideas aloud before writing, and connect every topic to California and the student's own community. Expect a short written product most days; use the rubrics and answer keys to grade, and check current figures (minimum wage, district maps, rates) against the official sites since they change.

weeks.prep: Print the Declaration of Independence (archives.gov), short excerpts of Hobbes's Leviathan (ch. 13) and Locke's Second Treatise (chs. 2, 9), Magna Carta clause 39, and the English Bill of Rights (1689). Skim them yourself first.
misconceptions: Thinking Hobbes and Locke agree because both use the 'state of nature.' Hobbes concludes people need an absolute sovereign; Locke concludes government is limited and exists to protect natural rights.
Believing the Declaration created the government. It justified independence; the Articles and later the Constitution created governments.
Assuming the Framers copied Athens. They feared direct democracy and borrowed more from the Roman Republic and English practice.

days.guide: Read the Hobbes and Locke excerpts aloud and make a two-column chart (state of nature, why form government, limits on government). The student writes a comparison paragraph; check that it names each thinker's conclusion.

questions.q: How does Hobbes describe life without government?
questions.a: 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a war of all against all, so people surrender rights to an absolute sovereign for security.

questions.q: Why do people form government according to Locke?
questions.a: To protect natural rights to life, liberty, and property; government rests on consent and can be replaced if it violates those rights.

days.guide: Explain Athenian direct democracy and the Roman Republic's elected representatives, Senate, and checks. The student charts features the Framers adopted or rejected.

questions.q: Which feature of the Roman Republic did the Framers adopt?
questions.a: Representative government (elected officials, a Senate) and a mix of checks among offices.

questions.q: Why did the Framers reject Athenian direct democracy?
questions.a: They feared it was unstable and open to majority passion; it also wasn't practical for a large country.

days.guide: Read Magna Carta clause 39 and the English Bill of Rights. The student highlights limits on the monarch and finds the matching U.S. provisions.

questions.q: What does Magna Carta (1215) clause 39 guarantee?
questions.a: No free man may be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land — the root of due process.

questions.q: Name two English Bill of Rights provisions that reappear in the U.S. Constitution.
questions.a: No excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishments (8th Amendment); right to petition (1st Amendment); no taxes without Parliament's consent (Congress's power to tax).

days.guide: Read the Declaration's second paragraph aloud and underline Locke's ideas. The student sorts the grievances into categories (taxation, courts, military, self-government).

questions.q: Which Lockean ideas appear in the second paragraph?
questions.a: Unalienable rights (life, liberty, pursuit of happiness), government by consent of the governed, and the right to alter or abolish a destructive government.

questions.q: Give one grievance about taxation and one about the military.
questions.a: 'Imposing Taxes on us without our Consent'; 'keeping among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislatures.'

days.guide: Give the quiz, then the 300-word response. Check that the response uses evidence from at least two documents. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: In what year was the Declaration adopted and who was its principal author?
questions.a: 1776; Thomas Jefferson.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Hobbes — absolute sovereign for security. 2) Locke — life, liberty, property; consent; right of revolution. 3) Magna Carta 1215, limits king, due process. 4) English Bill of Rights 1689. 5) Declaration 1776, Jefferson. 6) Rome — representative republic. Response rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear claim (usually Locke), evidence from the Declaration and one other document, explanation of influence, acknowledges other influences.

weeks.prep: Use the National Constitution Center's Interactive Constitution. Print Federalist 10, 51 (excerpts), 78 (excerpts), Brutus No. 1 (excerpt), and Tocqueville on 'tyranny of the majority.' Prepare the Unit 1 test and DBQ documents.
misconceptions: Reading Madison as anti-faction in the sense of banning parties. He argues you can't remove the causes of faction without destroying liberty, so you control its effects.
Thinking the Anti-Federalists opposed any national government. They feared a distant, consolidated government and demanded a bill of rights.
Confusing separation of powers with checks and balances. Separation divides functions; checks let each branch limit the others.

days.guide: List the Articles' weaknesses together. The student matches each to the Constitution's fix. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three weaknesses of the Articles and the Constitution's fix.
questions.a: No power to tax (Congress may tax); no regulation of interstate commerce (Commerce Clause); no national executive or courts (Articles II and III); amendments required unanimity (Article V three-fourths).

days.guide: Read Federalist 10 in chunks. The student explains Madison's argument in steps: definition, causes, cure. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a faction and why can't its causes be removed?
questions.a: A group united by an interest adverse to others' rights or the common good; its causes are sown in human nature and liberty, so removing them would destroy liberty.

questions.q: How does a large republic control faction?
questions.a: It includes many interests, making it harder for any one faction to form a majority and oppress others; representatives filter public views.

days.guide: Read 51 and 78 excerpts. The student diagrams checks and balances with an example for each arrow. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Explain 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
questions.a: Each branch is given the means and motive to resist encroachment by the others; 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'

questions.q: Why does Hamilton call the judiciary the 'least dangerous' branch?
questions.a: It has 'neither force nor will, but merely judgment' — no army or purse.

days.guide: Read Brutus No. 1 and the Tocqueville excerpt. The student explains how the Bill of Rights answered these fears. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Brutus fear?
questions.a: That a large republic couldn't work and the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses would let the national government swallow the states.

questions.q: What is 'tyranny of the majority'?
questions.a: Tocqueville's warning that a democratic majority can oppress minorities through law and public opinion.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test with a DBQ essay on how the Constitution limits government power. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three ways the Constitution limits government power.
questions.a: Separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism (also enumerated powers and the Bill of Rights).

weeks.assessment_key: Test key: Articles weaknesses/fixes; Fed 10 faction; Fed 51 checks; Fed 78 judiciary; Brutus fears; Tocqueville. DBQ rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = thesis naming specific limits (separation of powers, checks, federalism, Bill of Rights), uses 4+ documents with accurate interpretation, outside knowledge, explains why limits matter.

weeks.prep: Print the Bill of Rights. Set up iCivics 'Do I Have a Right?' Prepare 10 First Amendment scenarios and a short Kelo v. New London summary (Oyez).
misconceptions: Thinking the First Amendment protects all speech everywhere. It limits government, not private employers, and allows some limits (true threats, incitement, time/place/manner).
Believing the Bill of Rights originally applied to states. It limited only the federal government until incorporation through the 14th Amendment.
Confusing eminent domain with confiscation. The Takings Clause requires public use and just compensation.

days.guide: Read the First Amendment's five freedoms. The student classifies 10 scenarios; check reasoning for each. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Can a public school punish a student for a silent armband protest?
questions.a: Not unless it substantially disrupts school (Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969).

questions.q: Can a city require a permit for a large march?
questions.a: Yes — content-neutral time, place, and manner rules are allowed.

days.guide: The student builds the Amendments 2–8 chart with modern examples. Focus on 4th, 5th, 6th, 8th. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 4th Amendment protect?
questions.a: Against unreasonable searches and seizures; generally requires warrants with probable cause.

questions.q: Name three 5th Amendment protections.
questions.a: Grand jury indictment, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, due process, just compensation.

days.guide: Explain the 14th Amendment's due process clause and selective incorporation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is incorporation?
questions.a: The process by which the Supreme Court applied most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the 14th Amendment's due process clause, beginning with cases like Gitlow v. New York (1925).

days.guide: Discuss economic rights and Kelo. The student analyzes the ruling and the backlash. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Kelo v. New London (2005) decide?
questions.a: 5–4: taking private homes for economic development counts as 'public use' under the Takings Clause; many states then limited eminent domain.

days.guide: Play iCivics; give the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 9th Amendment say?
questions.a: Listing certain rights doesn't deny others retained by the people.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, petition. 2) 2nd: bear arms. 3) 3rd: quartering. 4) 4th: search/seizure. 5) 5th: self-incrimination, double jeopardy, due process, takings. 6) 6th: speedy public trial, counsel. 7) 7th: civil jury. 8) 8th: no cruel/unusual punishment, excessive bail. 9) 9th: unenumerated rights. 10) 10th: reserved powers. 11) Incorporation via 14th. 12) Kelo 2005.

weeks.prep: Print or open the USCIS civics test (uscis.gov). Note: the 2008 version has 100 questions; a 2025 revision expanded the bank — use whichever USCIS currently posts. Find California jury information (courts.ca.gov) and sss.gov. Line up an interview with a volunteer or nonprofit leader.
misconceptions: Thinking citizenship only means rights. Discuss obligations: jury service, obeying laws, paying taxes, Selective Service for men 18–25.
Believing civil society means government. Civil society is voluntary associations outside government.
Position essays that ignore the other side. Address the strongest counterargument.

days.guide: The student takes the civics test and researches naturalization requirements. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three requirements for naturalization.
questions.a: Usually 18+, lawful permanent resident for 5 years (3 if married to a citizen), good moral character, English and civics tests, oath of allegiance.

days.guide: Research jury duty and Selective Service. The student writes about why each matters. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who must register with Selective Service?
questions.a: Nearly all men ages 18 through 25 living in the U.S.

questions.q: Name two California juror qualifications.
questions.a: U.S. citizen, 18+, resident of the county, able to understand English.

days.guide: Read Tocqueville on associations. The student maps 10 local civic organizations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why did Tocqueville admire American associations?
questions.a: Americans formed voluntary groups to solve problems themselves, building civic skills and checking government.

days.guide: The student interviews a volunteer/nonprofit leader and writes notes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give two good interview questions.
questions.a: 'How does your group influence public decisions?' and 'What obstacles do you face?'

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and the position essay. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a thesis on rights vs. responsibilities.
questions.a: Rights depend on citizens accepting responsibilities like jury service, since rights like a fair trial require them.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test: citizenship requirements, obligations, civil society. Position essay (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear thesis, 2+ examples, counterargument.

weeks.prep: Print Article I. Look up your U.S. Representative (house.gov) and Senators (senate.gov) and their committee assignments in advance. Bookmark congress.gov.
misconceptions: Thinking senators represent districts. Each senator represents the whole state; representatives serve districts.
Treating the elastic clause as unlimited. 'Necessary and proper' powers must connect to an enumerated power (McCulloch).
Confusing the Speaker with the Senate's presiding officer. The Vice President presides over the Senate; the majority leader sets its agenda.

days.guide: Read Article I, Sections 1–3. The student charts qualifications, terms, and unique powers of each chamber; quiz orally. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give the age, citizenship, and term for House and Senate.
questions.a: House: 25, 7 years a citizen, 2-year term. Senate: 30, 9 years a citizen, 6-year term.

questions.q: Name a unique power of each chamber.
questions.a: House: originates revenue bills, impeaches. Senate: tries impeachments, confirms appointments, ratifies treaties (two-thirds).

days.guide: Model looking up a member's committees and votes on congress.gov. The student summarizes all three members. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many representatives does California have, and why?
questions.a: 52 (after the 2020 census) — House seats are apportioned by population.

days.guide: Read Article I, Section 8 and sort the powers. Discuss the elastic clause. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give one power in each category: money, commerce, defense.
questions.a: Tax and borrow/coin money; regulate interstate and foreign commerce; declare war and raise armies.

days.guide: Diagram congressional leadership and committees. Explain standing, select, joint, and conference committees. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who leads the House?
questions.a: The Speaker, elected by the House majority.

days.guide: Give the Congress quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many members are in the House and Senate?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) House 25/7/2 yrs; Senate 30/9/6 yrs. 2) 435 and 100. 3) House originates revenue bills, impeaches. 4) Senate tries impeachments, confirms, ratifies treaties. 5) Elastic clause = Necessary and Proper. 6) Speaker leads House; VP presides over Senate. 7) California has 52 representatives. 8) Committees do most bill work.

weeks.prep: Print Article V. Bookmark congress.gov bill tracker. Prepare a bill template.
misconceptions: Thinking most bills become law. The large majority die in committee.
Assuming the president can veto parts of a bill. There is no line-item veto for presidents (Clinton v. City of New York, 1998).
Confusing proposal and ratification of amendments.

days.guide: Flowchart the process: introduction, committee, floor, other chamber, conference, president, override. The student explains each step.

questions.q: How can Congress override a veto?
questions.a: Two-thirds vote in both houses.

questions.q: What is a pocket veto?
questions.a: If Congress adjourns within 10 days (excluding Sundays) of sending a bill and the president doesn't sign it, it dies.

days.guide: The student tracks one bill and records sponsor, committee, status. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where do most bills stall?
questions.a: In committee.

days.guide: Simulate a markup and floor vote. The student writes and defends a short bill. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens in markup?
questions.a: The committee debates and amends the bill before voting to report it.

days.guide: Read Article V; compare 19th, 26th, and the ERA. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How are amendments proposed and ratified?
questions.a: Proposed by two-thirds of both houses (or a convention called by two-thirds of states); ratified by three-fourths of states.

questions.q: What did the 19th and 26th Amendments do?
questions.a: 19th (1920) women's suffrage; 26th (1971) voting age 18.

days.guide: The student writes the 400-word reflection; give the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why did the Framers make lawmaking slow?
questions.a: To encourage deliberation and compromise and guard against hasty, factional majorities.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: veto override 2/3; pocket veto; most bills die in committee; amendment process 2/3 + 3/4; ERA failed to reach 38 states. Mock bill rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear purpose, sections, amendment record, vote tally, reflection.

weeks.prep: Print Article II. Pick a recent executive order on federalregister.gov. Gather Cuban Missile Crisis documents (DocsTeach, JFK Library). Set up iCivics 'Executive Command.'
misconceptions: Believing executive orders are laws. They direct the executive branch and must rest on the Constitution or a statute; courts can strike them.
Thinking the president can declare war. Only Congress declares war; the president is commander in chief.
Treating the bureaucracy as separate from the president. Departments are part of the executive branch.

days.guide: Read Article II; list formal powers. Discuss informal powers. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name four formal presidential powers.
questions.a: Commander in chief, make treaties (with Senate consent), appoint officials (with Senate consent), veto, pardon.

questions.q: What is the 'bully pulpit'?
questions.a: Theodore Roosevelt's term for using the presidency's visibility to persuade the public.

days.guide: Read the executive order; identify the legal basis and limits. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where does an executive order's authority come from?
questions.a: The Constitution (Article II) or powers granted by Congress through statute.

days.guide: Diagram the 15 executive departments; the student researches one independent agency. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name four executive departments.
questions.a: State, Treasury, Defense, Justice (also Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, HHS, HUD, Transportation, Energy, Education, Veterans Affairs, Homeland Security).

days.guide: Analyze Cuban Missile Crisis documents; evaluate Kennedy's options. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What options did Kennedy consider and choose?
questions.a: Airstrike, invasion, diplomacy, or a naval blockade; he chose a 'quarantine' (blockade) plus negotiation; the USSR removed missiles and the U.S. pledged not to invade Cuba (and privately agreed to remove missiles from Turkey).

days.guide: Give the quiz and play the game. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many executive departments are there?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: formal powers; executive orders; 15 departments; Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 blockade. Case study (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = options, risks, decision, evaluation with documents.

weeks.prep: Print Article III. Find a short confirmation-hearing clip (C-SPAN). Pick a recent Supreme Court opinion syllabus (supremecourt.gov). Prepare Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Supreme Court hears all appeals. It chooses a small share through certiorari.
Confusing the holding with the reasoning.
Assuming justices serve fixed terms. They serve during 'good behaviour' (life tenure).

days.guide: Diagram the federal courts; locate California in the Ninth Circuit. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many levels are in the federal court system?
questions.a: Three: district courts, courts of appeals (13 circuits), Supreme Court.

days.guide: Explain certiorari and the rule of four. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the rule of four?
questions.a: Four justices must vote to grant certiorari for the Court to hear a case.

questions.q: About what share of petitions are granted?
questions.a: Around 1% — roughly 60–80 cases from several thousand petitions per year.

days.guide: Watch a hearing segment; evaluate senators' questions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Senate's role?
questions.a: Advice and consent — confirms nominees by majority vote.

days.guide: Read a syllabus; identify question, holding, reasoning. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a 'holding'?
questions.a: The Court's answer to the legal question.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name one check on the judiciary.
questions.a: Senate confirmation, impeachment, constitutional amendments, or Congress setting jurisdiction.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) House 25/7/2; Senate 30/9/6. 2) Veto override two-thirds of both houses. 3) Amendment: two-thirds proposal, three-fourths ratification. 4) Commander in chief, treaties, appointments, veto, pardon. 5) Executive orders need constitutional or statutory basis. 6) 15 departments. 7) District courts → 13 courts of appeals → Supreme Court; California in the Ninth Circuit. 8) Rule of four; roughly 1% of petitions granted. 9) Senate confirms justices by majority. 10) One check on each branch. Scoring: 90%+ mastery, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% developing.

weeks.prep: Open Oyez summaries for Marbury v. Madison (1803), McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), and United States v. Nixon (1974). Print short essays on originalism and living constitutionalism (e.g., National Constitution Center).
misconceptions: Thinking judicial review is written in the Constitution. Marshall inferred it in Marbury.
Reading McCulloch as letting Congress do anything. It allows implied powers connected to enumerated ones.
Equating judicial 'activism' with a political side. Both liberal and conservative courts strike down laws.

days.guide: Read Marshall's key lines ('It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is'). The student explains the case's logic step by step.

questions.q: What did Marbury v. Madison establish?
questions.a: Judicial review — courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution; part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was void.

questions.q: Why was the ruling politically clever?
questions.a: Marshall denied Marbury his commission (avoiding a clash with Jefferson) while claiming a major power for the Court.

days.guide: Analyze McCulloch. The student explains both holdings. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What were McCulloch's two holdings?
questions.a: Congress could create a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause (implied powers); Maryland could not tax it, because 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy' and federal law is supreme.

days.guide: Listen to Oyez audio excerpts of Nixon. The student explains limits on executive privilege. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did U.S. v. Nixon decide?
questions.a: Unanimously (8–0), that executive privilege is not absolute; Nixon had to turn over the Watergate tapes. He resigned soon after.

days.guide: Read the philosophy essays; the student applies each to one case. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define originalism.
questions.a: Interpreting the Constitution according to its original public meaning when adopted.

days.guide: The student writes a 500-word case analysis. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How did Nixon strengthen checks and balances?
questions.a: It showed no president is above the law and the judiciary can check the executive.

weeks.assessment_key: Case analysis rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = accurate facts, question, holding, reasoning; clear explanation of effect on checks and balances; evidence from the opinion; 500 words.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts of Plessy (with Harlan's dissent), Brown, Tinker, Miranda, Gideon, Bakke. Find a summary of Prop 209 (1996). Prepare moot court roles and Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking Brown ended segregation immediately. Implementation was slow ('all deliberate speed,' Brown II 1955) and met massive resistance.
Thinking students have no free-speech rights at school or unlimited rights. Tinker protects non-disruptive expression; later cases allow limits.
Confusing civil rights (equal treatment) with civil liberties (freedoms from government).

days.guide: Compare Plessy and Brown, including Harlan's dissent. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) hold?
questions.a: 'Separate but equal' segregation laws were constitutional.

questions.q: What did Brown (1954) hold and why?
questions.a: Unanimously, that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,' violating equal protection; it cited harm to Black children's sense of status.

questions.q: What did Harlan write?
questions.a: 'Our Constitution is color-blind.'

days.guide: Analyze Tinker and a later case (e.g., Morse v. Frederick or Mahanoy v. B.L.). Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Tinker test?
questions.a: Schools may restrict student speech only if it causes or forecasts substantial disruption or invades others' rights.

questions.q: What did Mahanoy v. B.L. (2021) decide?
questions.a: A school violated a cheerleader's free speech by punishing her off-campus Snapchat post.

days.guide: Analyze Miranda and Gideon. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Miranda require?
questions.a: Police must warn suspects in custody of the right to remain silent and to an attorney before interrogation.

questions.q: What did Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) hold?
questions.a: States must provide lawyers to defendants in felony cases who can't afford one.

days.guide: Analyze Bakke and Prop 209. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Bakke (1978) decide?
questions.a: Racial quotas in UC Davis medical school admissions were unconstitutional, but race could be one factor.

questions.q: What did Prop 209 do?
questions.a: Banned race and sex preferences in California public education, employment, and contracting (1996).

days.guide: The student argues one side for 5 minutes; take the Unit 4 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong moot court argument?
questions.a: Clear legal question, precedent, and answers to judges' questions.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal'; Harlan: 'Our Constitution is color-blind.' 2) Brown (1954): segregated schools 'inherently unequal,' 14th Amendment equal protection. 3) Tinker (1969): substantial-disruption test. 4) Mahanoy (2021) protected off-campus speech. 5) Miranda (1966): warnings before custodial interrogation. 6) Gideon (1963): right to appointed counsel in state felony cases. 7) Bakke (1978): quotas unconstitutional, race may be one factor. 8) Prop 209 (1996) banned preferences in CA public institutions. Moot court rubric (4 = exemplary … 1 = beginning): 4 = states the legal question, cites the Constitution and 2+ precedents accurately, answers 'bench' questions directly, clear 5-minute delivery.

weeks.prep: Print Washington's Farewell Address excerpt. Bookmark FEC.gov and the Living Room Candidate archive. Find two recent polls with methodology.
misconceptions: Believing the Constitution creates parties. Parties developed despite founders' warnings.
Thinking Citizens United allowed unlimited direct contributions to candidates. It allowed unlimited independent expenditures; direct contributions remain capped.
Treating any poll as accurate. Check sample, margin of error, wording.

days.guide: Read Washington's warning. Trace party systems. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Washington warn about?
questions.a: The 'baneful effects of the spirit of party.'

questions.q: Name the first two parties.
questions.a: Federalists (Hamilton) and Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison).

days.guide: Explain primaries, caucuses, conventions, and California's top-two primary. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does California's top-two primary work?
questions.a: All candidates appear on one ballot; the top two vote-getters advance to November regardless of party (Prop 14, 2010).

days.guide: Analyze three campaign ads (e.g., 'Daisy' 1964, 'Morning in America' 1984). Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What technique does 'Daisy' (1964) use?
questions.a: Fear appeal — nuclear war imagery.

days.guide: Use FEC.gov; analyze Citizens United. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Citizens United v. FEC (2010) decide?
questions.a: Government can't limit independent political spending by corporations and unions; it led to super PACs.

days.guide: Evaluate two polls; take the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: A poll shows 48% vs 45% with ±3.5% margin. Is it a clear lead?
questions.a: No — within the margin of error.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Washington warned of the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party.' 2) First parties: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. 3) Top-two primary: top two vote-getters advance regardless of party (Prop 14, 2010). 4) Citizens United (2010): no limits on independent expenditures by corporations/unions; direct contributions still capped. 5) 48% vs. 45% with ±3.5% is within the margin of error. Ad analysis rubric (4 levels): 4 = identifies technique (fear, bandwagon, testimonial, etc.), target audience, message, and evaluates effectiveness with historical context for all three ads.

weeks.prep: Visit registertovote.ca.gov. Get a recent Official Voter Information Guide. Explore Citizens Redistricting Commission maps. Prepare Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking 16-year-olds can vote in California. They can pre-register; registration activates at 18.
Thinking the popular vote elects the president directly.
Confusing gerrymandering with apportionment.

days.guide: Walk through registration. Explain pre-registration. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: At what age can Californians pre-register?
questions.a: 16 or 17; they're automatically registered at 18.

days.guide: Read a proposition in the guide with LAO analysis and pro/con. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the LAO provide?
questions.a: Nonpartisan analysis of a measure's fiscal effects.

days.guide: Compare the 2003 and 2021 recalls. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happened in 2003?
questions.a: Gov. Gray Davis was recalled and Arnold Schwarzenegger elected.

questions.q: What happened in 2021?
questions.a: Gov. Gavin Newsom survived, with about 62% voting no.

days.guide: Explore redistricting maps; explain gerrymandering. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are 'packing' and 'cracking'?
questions.a: Packing concentrates opposing voters into few districts; cracking splits them across many.

questions.q: Who draws California's districts?
questions.a: The 14-member Citizens Redistricting Commission (Props 11 and 20) draws legislative maps; note that voters approved Prop 50 in 2025 to use legislature-drawn congressional maps temporarily — check current status.

days.guide: Calculate electoral votes and debate; take the Unit 5 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many electoral votes are there and how many to win?
How many electoral votes does California have (2024–2030)?

weeks.assessment_key: Ballot-measure analysis rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): summary, fiscal effect, both arguments, reasoned decision. Unit 5 test: parties, primaries, Citizens United, registration, recall, redistricting, Electoral College.

weeks.prep: Open the California Constitution (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and an LAO budget overview. Pick a current California bill to track.
misconceptions: Thinking federal law always wins. Federal law is supreme only within federal powers; states keep reserved powers.
Assuming the California Constitution is like the U.S. one. It is far longer and amended often.
Confusing the Assembly and Senate. The Assembly has 80 members with 2-year terms; the Senate has 40 with 4-year terms — like the U.S. House and Senate.

days.guide: Make a Venn diagram of powers; discuss the 9th and 10th Amendments. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name a concurrent power.
questions.a: Taxing, borrowing, making courts, enforcing laws.

days.guide: Analyze a federal-state conflict. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Gonzales v. Raich (2005) decide?
questions.a: Congress can prohibit homegrown medical marijuana under the Commerce Clause, even where state law allows it.

days.guide: Compare the two constitutions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How can the California Constitution be amended?
questions.a: By legislative proposal (two-thirds of each house) or initiative (signatures equal to 8% of the last gubernatorial vote), then majority voter approval.

questions.q: Name a right explicit in California but not the U.S. Constitution.
questions.a: Privacy (Article I, Section 1).

days.guide: Track a bill on leginfo. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many members in the Assembly and Senate?

days.guide: Give the federalism quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 10th Amendment reserve?
questions.a: Powers not delegated to the U.S. nor prohibited to states are reserved to the states or the people.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Federal: coin money, declare war, regulate interstate commerce; state: run elections, set up local governments, regulate intrastate commerce; concurrent: tax, borrow, make courts. 2) 10th Amendment reserves undelegated powers to states or people. 3) Gonzales v. Raich (2005): federal ban on homegrown marijuana upheld under the Commerce Clause. 4) CA amendments: legislature (two-thirds each house) or initiative (8% signatures), then majority vote. 5) Privacy is explicit in CA Const. art. I §1. 6) Assembly 80 members (2-year terms), Senate 40 (4-year terms). Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Get your city/county budget and a council agenda. Visit California Courts website. Research a California tribe's government.
misconceptions: Thinking the city provides everything. Special districts, counties, and school districts provide many services.
Misunderstanding Prop 13 as a cap on all taxes. It limits property tax rates (1%) and assessment increases (2%/yr until sale), which shifted local finance toward other sources.
Thinking tribes are subject to state government like counties. Tribes are sovereign nations with government-to-government relationships.

days.guide: Map who provides water, schools, police, fire, roads, parks. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a special district?
questions.a: A local government for one service, like water or fire.

days.guide: Analyze the budget; explain Prop 13. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Prop 13 (1978) do?
questions.a: Capped property taxes at 1% of assessed value and limited annual assessment increases to 2% until sale.

days.guide: Research a tribal government. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: About how many federally recognized tribes are in California?
questions.a: More than 100 (about 109).

days.guide: Diagram California courts. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name the three levels.
questions.a: Superior Courts (58, one per county), Courts of Appeal, Supreme Court (7 justices).

days.guide: Watch a meeting; write summary and public comment; take Unit 6 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How long is a typical public comment?
questions.a: Usually 1–3 minutes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) Special districts provide single services (water, fire). 2) Prop 13 (1978): 1% cap on property tax rate, 2%/yr assessment growth until sale, two-thirds vote for special taxes. 3) Tribes are sovereign with government-to-government relations; CA has about 109 federally recognized tribes. 4) CA courts: 58 superior courts, Courts of Appeal (6 districts), Supreme Court of 7 justices. Meeting report rubric (4 levels): 4 = accurate summary of agenda items and decisions, identifies who decided and how public input was used, a specific 1–3 minute public comment with evidence.

weeks.prep: Find a summary of NYT v. U.S. (1971). Pick a political story covered by three outlets. Gather 5 viral claims to fact-check.
misconceptions: Thinking prior restraint is always banned. It faces a heavy presumption against it.
Assuming any bias means a story is false. Framing shapes emphasis; check facts separately from tone.
Reading vertically (staying on one site) to check credibility. Lateral reading means leaving the site to see what others say about it.

days.guide: Analyze the Pentagon Papers case. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did NYT v. U.S. hold?
questions.a: 6–3, the government failed to justify prior restraint; the papers could publish.

days.guide: Compare three outlets' coverage. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is framing?
questions.a: How a story is presented — emphasis, word choice, sources.

days.guide: Practice lateral reading on five claims. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is lateral reading?
questions.a: Opening new tabs to check what other sources say about a site or claim.

days.guide: Analyze an official's social media and FDR's fireside chats. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What were fireside chats?
questions.a: FDR's radio addresses (1933–1944) speaking directly to Americans.

days.guide: The student writes a media-literacy guide; quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three steps to verify a claim.
questions.a: Check the source, read laterally, find the original.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) NYT v. U.S. (1971), 6–3: government failed to justify prior restraint. 2) Prior restraint = government blocking publication in advance. 3) Framing = choices of emphasis, words, and sources. 4) Lateral reading = leaving the site to check what others say about it. 5) FDR's fireside chats were radio addresses. Media-literacy guide rubric (4 levels): 4 = 5+ practical steps with examples (check the source, read laterally, find the original, check date, look for evidence), explains framing and bias vs. accuracy, clear voter audience.

weeks.prep: Print Freedom House reports for two countries. Find Mandela's 1964 Rivonia Trial speech excerpt.
misconceptions: Confusing federal and unitary systems. In a federal system power is constitutionally divided between national and state governments; in a unitary system the national government holds power and can create or abolish local units.
Thinking dictatorships arise only by force. Hitler gained power legally before dismantling democracy.
Treating Freedom House scores as precise facts. They are expert ratings.

days.guide: Compare systems and U.S. vs UK. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How is the head of government chosen in the UK?
questions.a: The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority in Parliament.

questions.q: Example of a unitary state?
questions.a: France or the UK.

days.guide: Analyze Germany 1933 and Chile 1973. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How did Hitler consolidate power?
questions.a: Appointed chancellor January 1933; Reichstag fire decree; Enabling Act (March 1933).

questions.q: What happened in Chile in 1973?
questions.a: A military coup led by Pinochet overthrew elected president Allende.

days.guide: Analyze the Mexican Revolution and 1917 constitution. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Whom did the revolution overthrow?
questions.a: Porfirio Díaz.

questions.q: Name two 1917 constitution provisions.
questions.a: Land reform (Article 27) and labor rights (Article 123).

days.guide: Read Mandela's excerpt. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What ideal did Mandela say he was prepared to die for?
questions.a: A democratic and free society with equal opportunities.

days.guide: Write a country comparison; quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are Freedom House's two categories?
questions.a: Political rights and civil liberties.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Unitary (UK, France) vs. federal (U.S., Mexico) vs. confederal (Articles of Confederation). 2) Parliamentary PM is chosen by the legislature's majority. 3) Germany 1933: Hitler appointed chancellor, Reichstag fire decree, Enabling Act. 4) Chile 1973: Pinochet's coup overthrew Allende. 5) Mexico: revolution against Díaz (1910); 1917 Constitution — land reform (art. 27), labor rights (art. 123). 6) South Africa's first multiracial election 1994, Mandela president. Comparison rubric (4 levels): 4 = Freedom House scores for political rights and civil liberties, specific evidence for each, explanation of differences.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts of King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963; King Institute at Stanford has the text). Help the student brainstorm local or state issues in advance and find the relevant decision-makers (city council, school board, legislators).
misconceptions: Thinking civic action means protest only. Letters, public comment, petitions, testimony, and volunteering are all civic action.
Choosing an issue too big to influence ('end climate change'). Narrow to a local decision with a clear decision-maker.
Not documenting the action. Keep copies, dates, photos, and any replies for the portfolio.

days.guide: Read the excerpts aloud, stopping at the just/unjust law passage. The student lists the tensions King addresses (law vs. justice, order vs. liberty, patience vs. urgency) with a quotation for each.

questions.q: How does King distinguish just from unjust laws?
questions.a: A just law squares with the moral law; an unjust law degrades human personality (e.g., segregation laws). One who breaks an unjust law must do so openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty.

questions.q: Whom does King criticize as a 'great stumbling block'?
questions.a: The 'white moderate' who prefers order to justice and tells activists to wait.

questions.q: Quote King's line about interconnectedness.
questions.a: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.'

days.guide: Model researching an issue from three perspectives (e.g., a local housing project). The student chooses an issue, summarizes at least three perspectives with sources, and names who decides.

questions.q: Why identify decision-makers before acting?
questions.a: So the action reaches the people with authority over the decision, making it effective.

days.guide: The student writes a plan: the action, audience, message, timeline, and how they'll document it. Review it for feasibility this week.

questions.q: Name four forms of civic action.
questions.a: A letter to a legislator, public comment at a meeting, a petition, and a volunteer project.

days.guide: The student carries out the action (sends the letter, delivers comment, completes volunteer hours) and documents it. Accompany them to any meeting.

questions.q: What counts as documentation?
